title: Tracking 2026 NFL hold-ins: Vita Vea resolves contract situation
summary: More on the four players who sat out portions of camp during their contract situations.
full_text:
While the 2026 NFL preseason  enters its second full week of play, there are no more prominent players who are waiting for their contract situations to sort out.

 Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea became the last star to end his hold-in, agreeing to a one-year extension on Wednesday. At the start of the 2026 NFL training camp season, there were four total players who were waiting on contracts decisions that swayed their decisions to practice. That list included:  Atlanta Falcons  running back Bijan Robinson , who signed a  historic deal , with  Detroit Lions  running back Jahmyr Gibbs  surpassing him with a  new contract  two days later.  Los Angeles Chargers  outside linebacker  Tuli Tuipulotu  is also practicing and said he'll play this season regardless of whether he gets a deal. 

 Let's take a look at how each situation came to a resolution.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Gibbs | Robinson | Vea | Tuipulotu 

 
 

 

 Vita Vea , DT, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Status: Agreed to a one-year extension 

 Aug. 19 update: The hold-in for Vea has ended, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter on Wednesday. Vea and his agent, Collin Roberts, reached an agreement with the Bucs on a one-year extension that sources said adds $6 million to the $18 million he was already set to make in 2026 for a total of $24 million, plus an additional $24 million in 2027. He'll make $30 million guaranteed, a source told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler.

 Aug. 7 update:  Vea still is not practicing because of a back injury and his contract dispute. He also wasn't on the practice field either. However, as of right now, Bowles expects him to travel with the team Monday to joint practices at the New York Jets .

 "Right now, yes, everybody's going," Bowles said.

 Aug. 6 update: The Buccaneers have "no plans" to trade Vea, according to general manager Jason Licht when asked Thursday about Vea's hold-in. Collin Roberts, Vea's agent, told the Tampa Bay Times this week that he "doesn't see it ending in anything but a trade."

 

 "We love Vita," Licht added. "We've been engaged with his agent recently. I don't know how it's gonna end, but we've been engaged and that's at least some progress." Vea has been present at the Bucs' facility, taking part in classroom instruction and observing practice from the sideline. He has also been seen helping coach teammates up during positional drills, but he isn't physically participating.

 Aug. 2 update: The star defensive tackle remains sidelined with a back injury, as well as his contract hold-in. Coach Todd Bowles said there is "nothing new" to report on his injury, and he is unsure if Vea will make the trip to the  New York Jets  for a pair of joint practices starting Aug. 11.

 July 31 update: Vea, who stayed indoors to receive treatment Thursday, was back out on the practice field Friday with teammates but was still sidelined with a back injury sustained during the team's conditioning test. Bowles said he does not have a timetable yet for Vea's back.

 July 30 update: While Vea was on the sidelines during Wednesday's first training camp practice and was standing alongside teammates during positional drills, he was not on the practice field Thursday. Bowles said Vea tweaked his back in the team's conditioning test Tuesday and he was getting treatment. Vea did, however, participate in an interview on the "Up & Adams Show," but he did not discuss his contract. Vea is set to earn $17 million this season, but none of it is guaranteed, along with a per-game roster bonus that is capped at $1 million total. Bowles said they are preparing for the season as if Vea will play. 

 -- Jenna Laine, Buccaneers reporter 

 

 
 

 Tuli Tuipulotu , OLB, Los Angeles Chargers 
 Status: Seeking a new contract, but planning to play

 Aug. 11 update: Tuipulotu said he'd play this season regardless of whether he gets a new deal. "I'll let my agents and the guys upstairs handle that. Let the business handle business. I'm a football player. That's all I do. That's all I know."

 Aug. 6 update:  Tuipulotu participated in team drills during Wednesday's padded practice, his second day in a row after not participating in team drills for the first six days of training camp.

 Tuipulotu looked like himself, bursting by the line of scrimmage to shut down running back Omarion Hampton on one of his first snaps and generating pressure throughout practice.

 Coach Jim Harbaugh originally said that Tuipulotu's absence was being "handled internally," then later said it was a "ramp up." Neither Tuipulotu, his representatives or the Chargers have acknowledged a contract-related absence, but his return to the field signals that whatever matter was being handled internally is resolved.

 Aug. 5 update:  Tuipulotu, who has been a limited participant in practice this training camp amid ongoing contract negotiations, was a full participant in Wednesday's practice. The caveat is that the practice was a walkthrough, so Tuipulotu and the other Chargers players were going at half speed. He still has yet to participate in a non-walkthrough practice 11-on-11 period, but his participation could be a sign that things could be headed toward a resolution.

 

 Aug. 4 update:  Coach Jim Harbaugh said Tuesday that Tuipulotu's absence from team drills remains part of "his ramp up." Harbaugh stopped short, however, of explaining any further, saying, "I don't know for sure where it's at. If I knew for sure, then I would say for sure."

 After noticing a reporter's facial expression, Harbaugh went on to explain he doesn't know exactly what's happening with Tuipulotu because he is not a medical professional.

 "Am I in somebody's body? A doctor? he said. "A lot of things that hang on my wall, but a medical degree is not one of them."

 Tuipulotu participated in one 7-on-7 rep but did not take part in the remainder of team drills on Tuesday, marking his sixth straight practice with limited participation as his contract situation remains unresolved.

 Aug. 3 update: Tuipulotu again did not participate in team drills, continuing his limited participation as his contract situation remains unresolved. The Chargers, Tuipulotu, and his representation remain mum about Tuipulotu's absence from practice, though it appears to be contract-related. Tuipulotu remains in good spirits and engaged throughout practice. His routine has been the same each day: he participates in individual drills, jokes with teammates, works with a trainer briefly, then watches practice with the team.

 Aug. 1 update:  Coach Jim Harbaugh declined to say whether outside linebacker Tuli Tuipulotu's absence from team drills at practice is contract-related, saying only the situation is being "handled internally" and repeatedly describing Tuipulotu as "ramping up."

 July 31 update:  Tuipulotu continued not to practice amid ongoing contract negotiations Friday. He went through individual drills, worked off to the side with a trainer and watched practice.

 July 30 update: The Chargers outside linebacker did not practice Thursday for the second straight day amid ongoing contract negotiations, but he did more on-field work with teammates than on the opening day of camp. Tuipulotu wore a helmet and jersey Thursday and went through individual drills with the team before working off to the side with a trainer. On Wednesday, he was in a T-shirt and shorts and worked off to the side with a trainer.

 -- Kris Rhim, Chargers reporter 

 

 
 

 Bijan Robinson , RB, Atlanta Falcons 
 Status: Signed a new deal 

 Aug. 4 update:  The two-time Pro Bowler and the Falcons reached agreement on a three-year extension worth up to $75 million that now will make him the highest-paid running back in NFL history, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

title: 2026 Carolina Panthers training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our updates from Panthers training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Panthers writer Mike Kaye will have the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Panthers camp. Will QB Bryce Young and the Panthers take another step forward after making the playoffs in 2025? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, concluding with the Panthers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- As Jaguars tight ends Brenton Strange and Nate Boerkircher made life difficult for the Panthers' defense Wednesday in joint practice, quarterback Bryce Young and wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan had some fun of their own on the opposite field.
 Young and McMillan were nearly automatic in foreign territory outside of EverBank Stadium. The quarterback heaved the ball down the field for his top target and McMillan routinely made him look good.

 The fireworks started with Young tossing a beautiful strike to McMillan as he beat cornerback Jabbar Muhammad to the end zone in 11-on-11 drills. A little while later, Young hit McMillan on a crossing route in front of defenders at the tip of the goal line for a contested touchdown grab.

 Finally, Young lifted a ball toward the end zone, about 25 yards, for McMillan, who jumped up to snag the ball over two defensive backs for a third touchdown.

 

 More observations: 

 
 The following players were sidelined during the joint practice: RB  Chuba Hubbard  (hamstring), NT Cam Jackson (concussion protocol), WR Ja'seem Reed (calf), CB Akayleb Evans (undisclosed), QB Haynes King (hamstring), CB  Will Lee III  (groin) and TE Darren Waller (onboarding). 
 Outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips and wide receiver Xavier Legette were pulled early from drills as a precaution due to minor injuries, according to coach Dave Canales. Phillips told the staff he was fine after hurting his wrist, while the team's medical staff cleared Legette after he got rolled up on in team drills. 
 Tight ends Feleipe Franks and Mitchell Evans both produced touchdowns in team drills. Franks caught an early touchdown off a throw from third-string quarterback Kyle Trask and then mocked the Jaguars fans in attendance with a celebration after the score. Young found Evans streaking wide open to the end zone on a roughly 50-yard completion for a touchdown. 
 It was a mixed bag for the Panthers' defense against quarterback Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville offense. But in the red zone drills, the Jaguars scored five consecutive touchdowns, including three completions in the end zone to tight ends. 
 Returning linebacker Devin Lloyd had a couple of nice moments with a stop against the run and a pass breakup that led to some jawing between both sides. Phillips had an early tackle for loss on running back Ameer Abdullah , which featured the free agent addition tossing the veteran to the ground. 
 Safety Nick Scott picked off Lawrence during team drills and cornerback Mike Jackson made an impressive two-handed pass breakup on wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr . in 11-on-11 work. 
 
 

 Monday, Aug. 17 
 New Panthers tight end Darren Waller 's free agency waiting game ended last Wednesday. He said his agent called him about the opportunity that morning right before he was heading out to a training session.

 Waller, who will turn 34 in September, didn't practice on Monday after officially signing with his fifth NFL team. Instead, he watched the workout, chatting with coaches and new teammates throughout the session.

 In Carolina, he is reunited with safety Tre'von Moehrig , whom he played with previously in Las Vegas, and outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips and associate head coach Darrell Bevell, whom he worked with in Miami last season.

 According to coach Dave Canales, Waller isn't likely to mix it up with the Jaguars in joint practices on Wednesday in Jacksonville. But the veteran playmaker might be able to suit up in his newly issued No. 35 jersey and get some individual work with starting quarterback Bryce Young .

 

 More observations: 

 
 Ja'seem Reed , a training camp wide receiver-turned-summer standout, sustained a calf injury against the Buffalo Bills on Saturday, according to Canales. He was set to undergo imaging on the ailment Monday after practice. 
 Outside linebacker Cam Gill played through a shoulder injury against the Bills, posting a sack in the second preseason game. He was held out of the first workout of the week due to increased soreness, according to Canales. 
 Rookie cornerback Will Lee III played through a groin injury against Buffalo but was sidelined Monday during practice. 
 The Panthers cross-trained offensive linemen during the workout. Rookie Albert Reese IV , who was signed as an offensive tackle, played second-team right guard, while veteran Jake Curhan worked with the second-team line as a left guard. Chandler Zavala , who had an underwhelming outing against Buffalo as the starting left guard, played second-team center. Backup center Nick Samac took his turn as the third-string right guard for the third time this summer. 
 The highlight of the hottest practice session to date was an intermediate sideline toss from Young to wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan over cornerback Akayleb Evans , who was wearing a red non-contact jersey. Young fit the ball perfectly in front of McMillan to grab it right before heading out of bounds. 
 Third-string QB Kyle Trask , who was signed last week, fired an excellent deep ball shot to depth wide receiver Casey Washington for a touchdown in 11-on-11 drills. 
 

 
 Who is the Panthers' top performer so far at camp? 
 Third-year wide receiver Jalen Coker 's immediate returns after receiving a three-year, $34 million contract extension in July have made the Panthers' brass look wise this summer. The former undrafted playmaker has gotten open with regularity and caught the ball cleanly and consistently throughout training camp.

 Coker has looked dynamic opposite Tetairoa McMillan , who has impressed in his own right. The top tandem's summer production has been encouraging, especially with third-round pick  Chris Brazzell II  (knee) out for the season and 2024 first-round pick Xavier Legette still working to live up to his draft pedigree.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 
 Will the offensive line be able to overcome a litany of injury adversity to begin the season?

 The Panthers' longtime starting tackles,  Ikem Ekwonu  (knee) and Taylor Moton (blood clot), will be sidelined into the regular season. They'll be replaced by free-agent addition Rasheed Walker at left tackle and first-round pick Monroe Freeling at right tackle, respectively. Walker has plenty of starting experience, but Freeling is switching to the opposite side of the line as a rookie.

 Left guard Damien Lewis (calf) and right guard Rob Hunt (back) missed several practices during the first few weeks of training camp. Brady Christensen , a versatile backup, will be an important insurance policy for both.

 

 Thursday, Aug. 13 
 The Carolina Panthers consider running back Chuba Hubbard to be "week-to-week" after he injured his hamstring in Wednesday's practice.

 Head coach Dave Canales said Hubbard underwent an MRI on Thursday before practice and the starting running back will be sidelined for the second preseason matchup against the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park, New York on Saturday.

 According to Canales, Hubbard sustained the injury during a one-on-one drill.

 With Hubbard sidelined, Jonathon Brooks and Trevor Etienne will rotate in with the starters for a couple of series, Canales…

title: Devin Lloyd wears green dot as badge of honor for Panthers' defense
summary: The ability to speak efficiently in the huddle is vital, and the fifth-year linebacker has impressed so far.
full_text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- When linebacker Devin Lloyd returns to Jacksonville to face the Jaguars on Friday at EverBank Stadium ( 7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN ) for the Carolina Panthers ' third game of the preseason, his helmet will not only be a different color but it will also have a new accessory attached to it.

 Lloyd will wear a green dot sticker on his helmet, an indicator of the headset inside, as the defense's vocal leader -- a responsibility the prized free agent rarely undertook during his four-year stint with the Jaguars.

 Lloyd, 27, earned second-team All-Pro and Pro Bowl nods in his final season in Jacksonville. He cashed in during free agency in March, signing a three-year, $41.9 million deal with the Panthers. And while the money serves as a nice incentive, Lloyd was looking for other things with his second NFL squad: a chance to win and that green dot on his helmet.

 "I always practiced wearing the green dot in Jacksonville," Lloyd told ESPN. "I played with the green dot in a couple of games -- shoot, I love it. ... That was a nonnegotiable in free agency."

 

 Lloyd is the middle man between coordinator Ejiro Evero, who enters his fourth season leading the Panthers defense, and the other 10 players on that side of the ball. Like the quarterback on offense, Lloyd receives the playcall from Evero and then relays that information to his fellow defenders.

 The ability to speak efficiently in the huddle is vital, and Lloyd has impressed his coaches and teammates with his voice.

 "We knew what we were going to get in terms of the on-the-field player, and we do our research, so we knew he was a quality guy, smart ... but the communication has been off the charts," Evero said.

 "It seems like it comes natural to him," veteran safety Tre'von Moehrig added.

 Lloyd's communication skills have extended beyond the defense. He has become a sounding board of sorts for offensive coordinator Brad Idzik as well. Idzik, who has been with Carolina since 2024 but will enter the 2026 season as an NFL playcaller, has exchanged information with Lloyd throughout camp to get the linebacker's insight into what he is looking at pre-snap and during plays.

 "I'm like, 'OK, what's giving it away that allows you to relate this receiver so quickly or this tight end so quickly? Help us get better, too,'" Idzik said. "He'll give me a little bit if it's not for the next practice -- not going to hold him back -- but I think going into the season those are going to be great conversations that carry over and help us as an offense."

 Lloyd played safety and wide receiver at Otay Ranch High School in Chula Vista, California, before converting to linebacker at Utah. While he boosted his profile well enough to be drafted at No. 27 by the Jaguars in 2022, he still had a learning curve at the position. His background at other positions and his 6-foot-3, 235-pound frame helped him stay fluid on the field, but the mental aspect was a long-term undertaking that Lloyd turned into an unwavering passion for the game.

 

 That dedication shined through during his breakout 2025 season as he produced 81 tackles, 1.5 sacks, seven pass breakups and five interceptions.

 And Lloyd's attention to detail was made apparent in his Panthers preseason debut against the Buffalo Bills on Saturday. He collected three tackles (one for loss) and a QB pressure in 12 snaps.

 "I was talking to him ... last week and I was like, 'Bro, what do you do outside of here?' cause he strikes me as a guy that is all football," Pro Bowl cornerback Jaycee Horn said. "And he's like, 'Nothing.'"

 An example of Lloyd's dedication to his craft and leadership took place last week. As the Panthers hosted an event for players and their families, Lloyd instead chose to spend time working on his tackle-shedding moves in a 25-minute post-practice work

 "He's got a real great urgency and focus about him," Panthers coach Dave Canales said.

 Lloyd credits his dedication as the primary reason for his ascension with awards and a lucrative free agent contract. His investment in improvement has made him a tough defender to fool, and he's able to play his own cat-and-mouse game with the quarterback because of his ever-evolving football IQ.

 The Panthers are hoping that Lloyd's presence, along with the addition of outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips , another top pickup, can improve last year's 16th-ranked defense.

 

 "Devin Lloyd is playing the game within the game, and he's trying to get a beat on your concepts, and he's usually dropping to a spot to start but then relating to receivers," Idzik said. "So, you've got to be wary of guys like that, where they run their white line on the page and they start to drift with the concept, so you can't always trust that he's going to be stagnant once he gets to the top of his drop."

 Lloyd and the rest of the Panthers' starters will have a healthy workload against his old teammates in Jacksonville during a joint practice on Wednesday. Following the shared workout, Lloyd will give the Jaguars a glimpse of what they let walk away in Friday's preseason matchup in his former stomping grounds.

 While Canales wouldn't commit to a playing time frame for Lloyd and other starters, Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence will get reacquainted with the linebacker throughout the week of work. Lloyd, who has turned himself into a versatile threat as a blitzer and a ball hawk, will need to be accounted for on every play against the Jacksonville offense.

 Lloyd admits there's a bit of emotion heading into his reunion with former teammates and coaches, but he's focused on getting better individually and as a team.

 "He just brings a leadership presence to the defense, and he's just about his business, so guys are going to follow behind him," Horn said.

 Lloyd has found his voice in Carolina, but he'll let his work do the talking against his former squad.

 "I'm grateful to be in the situation I'm in right now," Lloyd said. "Ultimately, what I do against them and what I do against other opponents, that'll all speak for itself."

title: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense works and 2026 expectations
summary: While Chicago's success will always be tied to its quarterback, a deeper look unveils the beauty of Johnson's offensive system and what really makes it go.
full_text:
When the Bears hired Ben Johnson last offseason, we had a pretty clear idea of who he was. The young coach had saved Jared Goff 's career and lit the Lions' offense aflame by grafting much of the old Sean McVay offense into a new approach in Detroit. His system included a ton of motion, play-action and intermediate in-breakers. All the classics ... with some new wrinkles, thanks to unique players such as  Jahmyr Gibbs and Jameson Williams  in the fold.

 So as Johnson took charge of second-year quarterback Caleb Williams , the burning questions were clear. How would Johnson reverse the arc for Williams, the 2024 No. 1 pick who had suffered as a rookie with late throws, missed targets, plenty of sacks and too many risks? How, if at all, could Williams play the pristine, timing-oriented ball that Goff had proved integral to Johnson's approach? Would Johnson lose patience with an oft-scrambling off-schedule playmaker?

 It's easy to look at the improvement of the Bears' offense in 2025 and say that our questions were well-founded. Williams' sack rate dropped from 10.0% to 3.8% (good job, Johnson), but his completion percentage fell from 62.5% to 58.1% (still inaccurate). The Johnson-Williams partnership must still be a work in progress. One with promise, but in progress nonetheless. Right? 

 The scope here is too narrow. It commits the most frequent error of our modern NFL discourse and analysis. It looks at everything through the lens of the quarterback, believing that the entire offense will only go as he goes and that all innovation is meant to directly impact his life. The Johnson offense resurrected Goff and looks as if it might boost Williams to elite heights -- but that's not the only thing it's doing.

 In fact, much of Johnson's first year in Chicago was not about Williams' game at all. The Bears' offense was stripped down to the studs and rebuilt anew, in a process Johnson knew would be painful and slow. But it worked. It set up the Bears for total team success -- not only in 2025 with a revitalized quarterback but for years to come with a complete system. And it started not on the air but on the ground.

 
 Getting the run game going 
 The Bears had the earliest possible bye week in 2025  -- Week 5 -- and were 2-2 entering it. There were big defensive issues to address (31st in success rate). On offense, they were about league average ... but with a major imbalance, ranking 12th in EPA per dropback and 31st in EPA per rush.

 "It was the running game," Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor told me. "We really needed to get the running game going."

 The running game is the lifeblood of Johnson's offense, and not in a trite, lip-servicey way -- a thing coaches say to placate their offensive linemen. Despite his new hat as the head coach, Johnson still installs the running game on a weekly basis himself, as he did in Detroit .

 

 "I haven't been around a playcaller, let alone a head coach, that installs his own running game," Bears tight end Cole Kmet said. "He has everybody in the room -- receivers, tight ends, backs, quarterbacks, linemen. We're all together as he installs."

 Johnson's heavy hand in the teaching of the run game is both a testament to its importance in his offense ... and its complexity. The Lions were notorious for running everything under the sun during Johnson's time as offensive coordinator, and he made a conscious decision before his first year in Chicago to install the offense as it was.

 Over three seasons in Detroit, Johnson's offense expanded in the stability offered by Goff, center Frank Ragnow and receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown . Fine adjustments are easier between longtime teammates, and new spinoffs of the playbook were written after the original chapters had long been internalized. Johnson didn't want to take the Bears' offense back to square one and rediscover those innovations, so he dumped it on their desks with the telltale thud of a thick textbook. But it was a lot to absorb in a short window, and through four weeks of Johnson's first season in Chicago, the running game proved difficult to stomach.

 The staff went back to the drawing board with their offensive linemen -- namely veteran guard Joe Thuney and center Drew Dalman. Thuney had played in two different offenses with different languages (New England and Josh McDaniels; Kansas City and Andy Reid) and could give Johnson and his staff honest feedback about the design of the rushing attack and how it was understood and communicated across the line. Dalman, as the center, was in charge of identifying the Mike linebacker -- off his point, the rest of the blockers would know their responsibilities. His understanding of the intent of the play and his authority to communicate it needed to be unquestionable.

 Here's a good snapshot of what it looked like pre-bye. In Week 4 against the Raiders, the Bears are down by five but in scoring range late in the fourth quarter. They want to run the clock as low as possible before they score a go-ahead touchdown.

 Before the snap, Raiders strongside linebacker Germaine Pratt (No. 57) is close to the line of scrimmage, and it has the Bears in an operational tizzy. Tight ends Kmet (85) and Durham Smythe (81) are requesting more information from the core of the formation, while both Dalman and Williams point.

 

 The Bears end up with three players (the center, left guard and left tackle) all on one defensive tackle while linebacker Devin White (45) runs unimpeded through the crease and meets D'Andre Swift behind the line of scrimmage. You can see the frustration from Thuney (62) and Dalman (52) after the play. Something got lost in translation.

 Remember, almost all of the Bears' offensive linemen were new to one another last season. A carousel of left tackles didn't help the building of chemistry -- but Thuney had never played beside Dalman, who had never played beside right guard Jonah Jackson , who had never played beside right tackle Darnell Wright . Kmet was a veteran at tight end, but fellow tight end Colston Loveland was a rookie. In fact, Jackson was the only one with experience in Johnson's offense. Though the old Lions running game accumulated over years of community growth, the Bears were trying to manufacture that in mere weeks.

 A lot of work in a little time can invite errors. In four games, the Bears had an appalling 11 pre-snap penalties (nine false starts, one illegal shift and one illegal motion). They were 31st in EPA lost on false starts and 30th in EPA lost on pre-snap penalties altogether. Not all of those penalties were on called runs, of course, but the Bears were actually breaking the huddle a whole second faster on called passes (19.6 seconds on the play clock) than they were on called runs (18.5 seconds). Many of Chicago's run calls were packaged with passes, and Williams could "can" one call to get to the other call. Again, no kid gloves on Johnson's offense. He wanted both calls available, and he was going to have them available.

 But the late assembly at the line, along with the time Williams needed to identify the defense and potentially change the call, was stressing a still-developing system. Johnson and his staff tried to alleviate the pressure by one-wording playcalls -- smashing each of them into one load-bearing keyword.

 "If we want to make this 10-word playcall into one word, we've still got to have something that's going to get the receivers the idea of where to line up, the line's going to understand the protection, the backs understand the action, the quarterbacks understand the read. It's on us to give as many mind taps as possible," Taylor said. "We came up with some pretty weird stuff."

 Every offense uses keywords like this to execute in the no-huddle. But to have up to 10 full playcalls on the one-word sheet for any given week -- calls in which the Bears could still motion, shift, kill a play, adjust an alignment, etc. -- and then to replace those with 10 new…

title: Hallmark, hot dogs and touchdowns: The Colston Loveland story
summary: The Bears' second-year tight end is making a name for himself on and off the field. Here's how.
full_text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- In a Chicago Bears offense that features the Madden cover man in quarterback  Caleb Williams  and a high-profile coach in Ben Johnson, the celebrity of one young player is emerging from the shadows.

 From landing a role in the Hallmark Channel movie "Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story," to slinging hot dogs at the famous "The Wieners Circle" this summer, second-year tight end  Colston Loveland  is gaining attention on and off the field.

 "He can do everything," Williams said.

 After leading the Bears in receiving (58 catches, 713 yards, six touchdowns -- all team highs) as a rookie, Loveland is ranked the No. 3 tight end in fantasy by ESPN, behind the  Arizona Cardinals ' Trey McBride and the Las Vegas Raiders ' Brock Bowers .

 "He can become the best tight end in the league," Williams said. "I think he is."

 But like with all elite players, Loveland isn't heading into Year 2 satisfied with his accomplishments.

 

 When Johnson popped by a special teams meeting early in training camp, he heard someone unexpected firing off questions at coaches.

 It didn't matter to Loveland that he wasn't likely to be on this specific unit given his sweeping role on offense. If there were ever a question about his responsibility on punt return or the field goal block team, Loveland made sure he would have the answers in his notes.

 "He's just a sponge right now," Johnson said. "He wants all the information. He knows all this knowledge is going to make him a better player, and he's going to continue to play faster."

 Once an install has been drilled down for the 10th time, Loveland will shift focus from his job at tight end to what's being asked of the wide receivers around him. He wants to know everything from the specifics behind route combinations -- even when he's not the primary target -- to the blocking rules for himself and the offensive line.

 "I don't want anyone to have an edge on me. Meaning, I want to study just as much or more than everyone," Loveland said. "I want to get as (many) touches, you know, whatever it may be.

 "So yeah, it's just like I see other people doing it, it's like, 'Why am I not doing it?'"

 That approach fuels Loveland on the practice field, where he routinely catches 100 passes from a combination of Bears quarterback and the Jugs machine before every camp session. 

 One catalyst for Williams' hot start to training camp was the target he looked to most often.

 

 During a two-minute drill at the end of practice July 31, Williams found Loveland four times on a drive that started at the offense's 39-yard line and culminated with Loveland corralling a tight-window pass in the end zone for a 14-yard touchdown.

 That moment didn't teach Williams anything he didn't already know about the former No. 10 pick who turned eight catches into 137 yards and a critical 2-point conversion in the Bears' 31-27 comeback win over the Packers in the playoffs.

 Williams had long recognized Loveland's potential as a weapon who "can do everything," the type of player whose big-play prowess has bailed the Bears' offense out of a bind.

 In one of many furious late-game rallies that defined the Bears' 2025 season, Loveland turned six catches into 118 yards and two scores in Cincinnati, including a 58-yard walk-off touchdown.

 "Put it up there and give him a shot," Williams said. "He's such a big target, easy target, runs the right routes and nice routes, and then other than that he can run block and disguise things. He's an all-encompassing tight end."

 Loveland outperformed most veterans at his position last season, ranking second among all tight ends in receiving yards from Weeks 9-18 and generating a +44.6 receiving EPA, per Next Gen Stats, which was the highest mark by a rookie tight end since 2016.

 Like Sam LaPorta did in Detroit under Johnson's leadership, Loveland's impact on the offense sparked one of the league's most explosive passing attacks. His on-field contributions carried the Bears past a slow start in 2025 to their first playoff victory in 15 years.

 "He just got a lot of versatility," linebacker  D'Marco Jackson  said. "He's a good route runner, he's loose. He's really good at the catch point, his radius.

 "Man, he's a good all-around player and I feel like he's going to be a challenge in camp to keep working with and good preparation for the season."

 Loveland is such a good route runner that WR1 Rome Odunze said he has "learned a lot from him."

 "Rare," Odunze said when asked about Loveland's versatility. "A diamond. It's impressive just to see his route-running ability. It's incredible. And then you get him down blocking and he's holding his own like he's a tackle.

 "So his versatility is truly incredible. I'm super glad that he's on the crew, and I learned a lot from him as well just from his movement and his fluidity in and out of his routes."

title: Shedeur Sanders not feeling pressure about Browns' QB decision

title: Is Cowboys' DaRon Bland finally over his nagging foot issue?
summary: Bland set an NFL record in 2023 with five pick-sixes and hopes to get back to form in 2026, boosted by some new shoes.
full_text:
OXNARD, Calif. --  DaRon Bland 's feet tell his story.

 A cornerback's success has more to do with feet than anything else. Backpedaling at the snap. Driving on a throw from the quarterback. Sprinting stride-for-stride with a wide receiver.

 If the footwork isn't good, then a cornerback will be in trouble.

 But what about when a foot isn't healthy? What then?

 Late in the 2024 training camp, Bland had surgery on his left foot to repair a fifth metatarsal stress fracture and missed the first 10 games of the season. He never felt quite the same as he had his first two years when he intercepted 14 passes and set an NFL record with five pick-sixes in 2023.

 

 Last season, the 2022 fifth-round pick was placed on injured reserve with three games remaining and had his second left foot surgery in as many years. In January, Dr. David Porter, a consultant for the Indianapolis Colts , replaced the screw in Bland's foot. He rehabbed throughout the offseason with the idea of being 100% ready for training camp.

 "It's a lot better," Bland said. "I mean I don't really feel no aches or pains that much. Little soreness here and there, but nothing major."

 Bland's movements appear sharper than last year. His quickness is better. He looks more confident.

 "I'm definitely getting a lot more push now getting out of my breaks," Bland said. "Not worried about it."

 

 Bland has made one change that he believes has helped his foot. He is wearing size 15 cleats instead of a size 14.

 "It's just us trying different things and trying to see what's best," Bland said. "So far this has felt the best right now."

 It doesn't matter to the Cowboys whether it's comfort or confidence. They need Bland, who signed a four-year, $90 million extension in 2025, to find the form of his first two seasons in new coordinator Christian Parker's scheme.

 As much as Bland's foot has been rebuilt, Schottenheimer does not believe there is a need to rebuild Bland's confidence because he showed his capability with 14 interceptions in his first two seasons.

 During that same stretch, he allowed seven touchdowns and a 60% completion rate in 877 coverage snaps, per ESPN Research. In his past two seasons with the foot injury, he allowed 10 touchdowns and a 65% completion rate in 687 coverage snaps.

 Bland returned his lone interception last season 68 yards for a touchdown.

 "DaRon doesn't say much, but he's extremely confident," Schottenheimer said. "He can't do what he's done in this league, even as a young, young player and not be pretty confident."

 

 This year, Bland has a third different position coach in as many seasons with Derrick Ansley, who came over from the Green Bay Packers . Given Parker's background with defensive backs -- coaching Pat Surtain II with the Denver Broncos , and Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean with the Philadelphia Eagles , plus Ansley -- Schottenheimer sees technical improvement in Bland.

 "I think he's really taken to the fundamentals in the scheme," Schottenheimer said. "But just really the way DA and those guys are coaching him, you see him flashing with the quick decisions and the quick breaks and the PBUs [pass breakups]. But I really like watching him too with the crack replaces, coming up and filling on runs, and things like that."

 While some cornerbacks can be loud and brash, Bland is reserved and quiet. When asked what he liked about Bland's camp, Ansley first mentioned his leadership and the tutoring he is doing with second-year cornerback Shavon Revel Jr.  Ansley said Bland is a "relationship guy" and an "observer."

 "You can tell why he's been All-Pro," Ansley said, "because he doesn't get rattled. He makes a play, he's the same guy. He gives up a play, he's the same guy. That's a characteristic that you need at corner because your life out there, you're walking on landmines, and at some point you're going to step on one and it explodes. You've got to be able to come back to life."

 Teammates, coaches and front office personnel have told him they see a difference between this year and last year. More importantly, he feels a difference.

 "Definitely sometimes you be in your head about this," Bland said.

title: 2026 Dallas Cowboys training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Cowboys training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Cowboys reporter Todd Archer has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at the Cowboys' camp. Will Dallas turn around the NFL's worst defense from 2025? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Cowboys' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Cowboys camp 
 
 Miller to play 15th season after getting 1-year deal from Cowboys 
 Sources: Cowboys, Quinnen Williams reach 3-year, $105.9M deal 
 Cowboys' Dak Prescott not shying away from setting lofty goals 
 Jones optimistic about Cowboys, likes 'what we put together' 
 Source: Ex-Cowboys QB Will Grier returns as offensive assistant 
 Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 

 Training camp opened with the Cowboys wanting a competition at left tackle between Tyler Guyton and Nate Thomas , but it never really materialized in part because of how well Guyton has performed.

 In the past two days, coach Brian Schottenheimer and offensive coordinator Klayton Adams spoke about the other side of the line and the right tackle situation, where Terence Steele is the starter.

 "T-Steele's got to play a little bit more consistent," Schottenheimer said. "He has had a couple days where he's been a little bit dropping his pads and getting edged a little bit. He needs to be better."

 Adams wonders if by working less, Steele will benefit. Steele, entering his seventh season, has played 2,333 of a possible 2,357 snaps the past two seasons.

 "He and I had a good conversation about that this morning of how we continue to try to find consistency," Adams said. "He's a guy that's going into Year 7, and he's never going to ask for a day off. He's never going to ask for a break. So we're just searching for ways to help him and help him play at his best and most consistently."

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 

 Amid the fights and skirmishes between the Cowboys and Saints, there was actually some practice, but not enough for coach Brian Schottenheimer's liking.

 On the first play between the offense and defense, there was a shoving match. On the fifth snap between the first-teamers, there was a fight. But let's stick to football, specifically the Cowboys' first-team offense against the Saints' defense.

 Unofficially,  Dak Prescott was 20-of-25 with one interception. On a crosser to CeeDee Lamb , the pass sailed over Lamb and right into the arms of safety Julian Blackmon . Prescott had a deep completion near the sideline to George Pickens that drew loud cheers from the fans.

 In red zone work, Prescott had touchdown passes to tight end  Jake Ferguson on a shovel pass, a quick throw to Pickens on a slant and a perfectly placed ball to the post that was high enough that only receiver  Ryan Flournoy could come down with the catch. Pickens was flagged for a celebration penalty by the officials when he flipped the ball in the direction of Saints cornerback  Kool-Aid McKinstry .

 "I think we're finding our rhythm," Schottenheimer said. "I'll go back to the preseason game. I think we kind of found our rhythm even in the second half against Seattle. And that's what training camp is for."

 

 Who is the Cowboys' top performer so far at camp? 

 George Pickens . He has essentially made a big play in every practice as he gets set to play on the $27.3 million franchise tag. Whatever disenchantment some might have expected from Pickens without a long-term deal has not materialized. Coaches have noted his attention in the meeting rooms since the start of training camp.

 He and Dak Prescott have picked up where they left off in 2025 when the receiver had career highs in catches, yards and touchdowns. Does that mean he will surpass those figures again in 2026? Not necessarily, but his performance so far has shown a focused player as the season inches closer.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 

 Because the Cowboys aren't going to play their starters in the preseason, it's impossible to completely answer anything about the defense. There have been encouraging signs there, but let's look to the offense for what can be answered in the preseason games: Who will back up Prescott?

 Joe Milton III and Sam Howell have alternated as Prescott's backup in practice and both have had good moments and not-so-good ones. The Cowboys believe they have line play and skill players to give both QBs a fair shot to perform in the preseason and not have them running for their lives. Read more below:

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 

 For the second time this month, the Cowboys will hold a joint practice, hosting the New Orleans Saints  on Tuesday after traveling to the Los Angeles Rams a week ago.

 The importance of the work isn't lost on tight end Jake Ferguson , who, like the rest of the Cowboys' starters and regulars, will not play in any of the three preseason games.

 "It's usually their starting defense going against our starting offense," Ferguson said. "That's where we get a good read of what we're looking like, what we're feeling like, what we need to clean up. We had that one against the Rams and came out firing. It was a lot of things we needed to clean up, but this is a good tell."

 The Saints will bring a familiar face with coach Kellen Moore. Ten years ago, Moore was Tony Romo 's backup for Dallas before breaking his ankle early in training camp. It helped pave the way for Dak Prescott to become the starter. Moore became a Cowboys assistant coach and served as offensive coordinator from 2019 to 2022. Moore also interviewed for the Cowboys head coaching vacancy that went to Brian Schottenheimer.

 "Kellen and I have kind of laid it out," Schottenheimer said. "It'll be similar to what we did with the Rams. A few less reps since they have another joint practice coming up [with the Rams], but you'll see a lot of the same situational work, some of the special teams stuff."

 More observations: 

 Monday's practice was conducted in helmets and jerseys, with no shells or pads, since the players were just two days removed from a preseason game. With the late return from Seattle, the Cowboys could not meet until late in the morning, and they held a practice that ran about 75 minutes.

 A sign the starters will get most of the work versus New Orleans: The backups had only 12 reps in practice; the starters had 30.

 Jaydon Blue was the only running back to not take any snaps during practice. He went through individual drills, but he is dealing with a shoulder injury. Phil Mafah (chest) did not get a carry, but he caught one pass. The bulk of the work went to Javonte Williams , Malik Davis and Israel Abinkanda .

 

 Friday, Aug. 14 

 Most of the regulars will not play in Saturday's preseason opener against the Seattle Seahawks , but there is one important position that could start to take shape: backup quarterback.

 Throughout training camp, Joe Milton III and Sam Howell have alternated days as Dak Prescott 's backup as they compete to be the No. 2.

 "It's been a very highly competitive contest," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "I think Joe's talent and ability to throw the football and athleticism jumps off the practice field when you see it. I think Sam's doing a great job of moving the team. But at the end of the day, the preseason games, they're going to play really the entire preseason, and that's where the bulk of the evaluation will be."

 Schottenheimer said there has been a back and forth between the quarterbacks. Milton served as Prescott's backup last year,…

title: 2026 Denver Broncos training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Broncos training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Denver Broncos camp is taking place in Englewood, Colorado, and Broncos reporter Jeff Legwold has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Broncos camp. We will update this file often as we track the Broncos' push toward getting to the Super Bowl after falling one game short last season. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Broncos camp 

 
 Who will line up at DT next to QB hit king Zach Allen? 
 Why 2026 is a crucial season for Bo Nix and the Broncos 
 Payton to talk to Taysom Hill about interest in Broncos 
 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 
 The folks crammed into the bleachers on Wednesday saw something that almost never happens -- All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II getting beat for a touchdown. Such is the expectation level for Surtain, a two-time first-team All-Pro and the NFL Defensive Player of the Year in 2024, that Jaylen Waddle 's catch-and-run touchdown in team drills was a remember-when moment. Quarterback Bo Nix had said earlier in camp he had tried to throw Surtain's way occasionally in drills, unlike the previous two years, and joked that "I don't mind throwing his way and getting an incompletion.''

 On Wednesday, Nix hit Waddle after a double move, as the quarterback placed the ball just out of Surtain's reach. After practice Surtain called Waddle's explosiveness a "unique skill" and that "he can take a 5-yard play and turn it into a 70-yard touchdown."

 More observations: 

 
 Coach Sean Payton said he had not made any definitive playing time decisions for the team's starters in Friday night's preseason game against the Green Bay Packers , but that he expected Nix's splaying time would be roughly a "14-snap count.'' Payton said he expected all three quarterbacks would play. 
 Payton said he went over the heated skirmishes in Tuesday's practice in a team meeting later that day. He reminded players that officials can now ask the league's replay center in New York to review any fights in a game to see if any players could be ejected, that on-field officials can get a ruling "and remove a player." Payton, who has repeatedly said practice fights are basically losses of discipline that can result in defeats in games, said he also told the players: "Let me know the game where we're fighting and then obviously we're not as concerned about winning that game, and then I'll kind of measure up the (other) head coach and see where we go, and we can all get ejected -- the games are too important." 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 The Broncos might be a business-like, veteran team with aspirations that reach well beyond an August practice, but emotions finally boiled with several skirmishes during team periods. The emotional temperature rose, as some pushing and shoving later turned into celebrations after each play in a red zone period. That later turned into a full-blown mass of humanity during an 11-on-11 period.

 Among the incidents were quarterback Bo Nix firing a ball at a defender after Nix had been knocked to the ground. Nix and edge rusher Nik Bonitto got entangled, with offensive tackle Mike McGlinchey having to be restrained as coaches tried to separate the players.

 

 "I love it,'' Nix said. " ... It's a physical game played by physical people. ... Practice gets long and the intensity gets high."

 Coach Sean Payton is well known for his stance against practice fights, feeling that a loss of discipline in practice results in a similar loss of discipline in games. Tuesday's skirmishes were the most significant of this camp.

 "It's gonna happen, [but] it just can't cross the line," offensive coordinator Davis Webb said. " ... I'm glad we're fiery, I love the competition out here ... [but] we can't cross the line."

 Webb added that Payton will certainly have something to say to the team at the conclusion of practice.

 More observations: 

 
 McGlinchey, who had two penalties (ineligible player downfield and a holding flag) in his 25 snaps played in the preseason opener , was pulled out of the formation after a false start penalty. McGlinchey finished the 11-on-11 period with the second-team offense. "It's not our standard,'' Webb said. " ... If it's not up to our standard you can be taken out.'' 
 Linebacker Drew Sanders was held out of practice for the second consecutive day. Center/guard Calvin Throckmorton left practice after the big skirmish with what looked like a cut above his left eye. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 
 Rookie running back Jonah Coleman continues to work his way up the depth chart toward a spot in the regular-season rotation, so much so that coach Sean Payton gave Coleman a fairly quick hook from the preseason opener. Coleman played 12 snaps Friday night in Atlanta and had four carries for 24 yards, with his last carry coming with 47 seconds left in the first quarter. Payton said he's seen enough from Coleman on the practice field to get the rookie out of the preseason opener that early.

 "I kind of felt it ... and there was a point when he got like two or three carries and I'm like 'alright, I've seen enough,'" Payton said. "I didn't need additional evidence of what I've been seeing for three weeks.''

 Coleman continues to get practice snaps with the first- and second-team offenses in camp in a variety of situations.

 More observations: 

 
 Inside linebacker Levelle Bailey suffered a fractured leg in the win over the Falcons, so the Broncos might be on the hunt for depth to finish out the preseason. Seventh-round rookie Red Murdock played the most defensive snaps in Friday's game (47) and continues to close in on a roster spot. Karene Reid (28 snaps) tipped the pass that cornerback Jahdae Barron returned 97 yards for a touchdown and undrafted rookie Taurean York played 22 snaps. Payton said "we'll see" when asked if they would add an inside linebacker, adding it was too soon to know if Bailey would be able to return this season. 
 Linebacker Drew Sanders played in his first game Friday since the playoff loss in Buffalo to close out the 2024 season -- he finished with a sack in 13 snaps against the Falcons. Sanders was held out of Monday's practice and worked on a side field. 
 Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle return to practice Monday and worked in team drills. Wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr . also returned to practice but worked on a side field after individual drills. 
 

 

 Who has been the Broncos' top performer at camp so far? 

 It is a close race between two receivers, second-year man Pat Bryant and Marvin Mims Jr ., with Bryant getting the nod in part due to Mims being slowed recently by a leg injury suffered last Friday.

 Mims started camp with a flourish, creating impact plays until he was limited by a soft-tissue injury that knocked him out of practice for a couple days. Bryant swooped in to be the big-play creator in Mims' absence. Bryant continues to ascend with precise routes and a seemingly fanatical desire to win the ball in the air every time. And on a team where most of the depth chart is settled, his efforts have been the most noteworthy.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 

 The Broncos suddenly have an issue at center, as starter Luke Wattenberg and backup Alex Forsyth have missed significant practice time with injuries while the No. 3 center -- Michael Deiter -- suffered a season-ending thigh injury this past week. It has put Calvin Throckmorton , who has gotten far more work at guard in his…

title: Who will fill the Broncos' DT spot next to Zach Allen?
summary: Allen and John Franklin-Myers collapsed pockets up the middle last season, but Denver now has to replace JFM. Can Allen keep up his elite play without him?
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- If things go right this season for Denver Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen , he might have to rename his dream beach house.

 Allen, who earned first-team All-Pro honors in 2025 and became only the second player to have 40 quarterback hits in back-to-back seasons (joining three-time Defensive Player of the Year J.J. Watt), has joked about calling his future oceanside residence the " John Franklin-Myers House" because of all the help Franklin-Myers provided him, allowing Allen to accumulate punishment on opposing passers.

 Allen has gone from a player who had two sacks in his first two NFL seasons combined with the Arizona Cardinals to a foundational player on a Super Bowl hopeful, someone the Broncos deemed important enough to give a four-year, $102 million extension to last summer. But he's also at the nexus of one of the Broncos' few offseason questions: Who will replace Franklin-Myers and help Allen do what he does best?

 Franklin-Myers, who played a little more than 500 snaps in each of the past two seasons, signed with the Tennessee Titans in free agency and is just one of two starters from the AFC Championship Game not on this Broncos roster in training camp (linebacker Dre Greenlaw being the other).

 

 "It'll be a little different this year," Allen said after a recent practice. "But we still have our guys, our room is still our room, we're still putting in the work, we still have big goals. D.J. [Jones] , Malcolm [Roach] , [ Eyioma Uwazurike ], young guys like Tyler [Onyedim] and Sai'vion [Jones] , there's no reason our standard shouldn't always be our standard."

 Allen and Franklin-Myers consistently created discomfort to the point of making Allen the answer to a rather intriguing trivia question. It was Allen, not any of the league's elite edge rushers, who led the league in quarterback hits in 2025. His 47 led by a healthy margin, as he was the only player credited with more than 40.

 That's a long way from being a former third-round pick who thought he was doomed after injuries and a position switch early in his career.

 "I thought I was getting cut -- people saying 'this kid's a bust' or whatever, but the NFL thing is like a math problem, you've [got] to figure it out," Allen said. "You can have great people around, telling you the right things and helping you -- like [Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph] has been so big for me -- but in the end what you put into it is going to come out. ... Discomfort can open your eyes, and my eyes were really open."

 Allen dishes out discomfort for quarterbacks in a defense that has led the league in sacks in each of the past two seasons. And Joseph watched his journey from the beginning.

 "I was with Zach from his rookie year to now, and he's gotten bigger and stronger over time, he's played the run game better [and] his rush I.Q. has gotten better," Joseph said. "... That's the toughest thing for players when they have success. Can they go back to the drawing board and improve?

 "If you're not improving in this league, people are going to catch you ... He's one of those special guys [who] doesn't want to get caught."

 The Broncos want to help continue that by finding a successor for Franklin-Myers on their 3-4 front. They have three former midround picks vying for the role opposite Allen. Emerging are Uwazurike (2023 fourth-round pick) -- who missed his rookie season due to a gambling suspension  -- Sai'vion Jones (2025 third-round pick) and Onyedim (2026 third-round pick). Uwazurike, who started the preseason opener in Atlanta, has consistently drawn raves for his progress from a bit player last season.

 

 "I've seen a guy who changed his body," Joseph said of Uwazurike. "He's always been a big man, but he's leaned out and he's moving very well. ... He's changed his body and now he's a different player. He's always wanted it, always been a run stopper for us and [now] he's a pass rusher."

 Onyedim has shown quickness at the point of attack in practice while his length (an offensive tackle-like 81⅜ inches) can help him shed blockers on the interior. Like Uwazurike, Jones has gained more power in the offseason.

 Whoever wins Franklin-Myers' old role will be tasked with taking attention off Allen. Unlike edge rushers, who usually rush in the quarterback's peripheral vision, Allen is in the middle of the pocket. He said he'd like to continue to pile up wins and QB hits next to his new running mate.

 "Sure, I'd like those to be four sacks a game," Allen said. "But if you beat the guard right away and the quarterback sees you clearly, that ball's out. ... So, a QB hit means you got there in time, that I'm productive, it means I'm helping Nik [Bonitto] and our edge guys ... and I hope it helps us win, because that's probably the number we all care about the most."

 The Broncos also hope the new sidekick can help the All-Pro manage his snaps. Allen topped 80% of the Broncos' defensive snaps in his first two seasons with the team, with more than 900 snaps each year -- an astounding number for an interior defensive lineman. Denver was slightly more judicious last season, when Allen played 797, and the team is trying to find a balance between keeping him rested and maximizing his impact.

 "He has tremendous stamina, so play 38 looks like (play) eight, play 60 still looks like eight," Broncos coach Sean Payton said. "So that's a big asset at a position where it's hard."

title: Why Lions, NFL coaches believe Super Bowl chances are possible
summary: If you don't believe Campbell & Co. that the Lions will be contenders, ask Sean McVay, Matt LaFleur and others.
full_text:
DETROIT -- When Dan Campbell arrived for the NFL's annual league meeting in March, no one would have guessed he was three months removed from one of his most disappointing seasons as the  Detroit Lions ' coach.

 Instead, those who saw him at the Arizona Biltmore in Phoenix were more preoccupied with his hair, which along with his goatee was considerably longer than anyone covering the team since 2021 could remember.

 "You know what? I just haven't cut it," Campbell joked. "I haven't cut it. I cut the sides, but I haven't."

 

 His relaxed look mirrored the calm confidence with which he discussed his team while answering questions from reporters alongside his coaching peers. He talked about his team heading into the 2026 season -- expressing his belief in the staff and the roster that he and general manager Brad Holmes had built.

 "We've been going. It's been fun. Been fun. Brad and I have been -- we've been back in the bunker just going at it," Campbell said. "It's been fun. It really has. Kind of a little bit of a rebirth, actually."

 His Lions were in need of the mini reset. They had won 15 games in 2024 and 12 the season before that, cementing themselves as one of the NFC's top contenders along the way. But in 2025, after losing both coordinators and eight coaches overall, they won just nine games and missed the playoffs for the first time since 2022.

 This offseason, some change was inevitable. The biggest: Campbell brought in former Arizona Cardinals offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to replace John Morton, whom the Lions fired in January after the first-time OC struggled to give Detroit an offensive identity. Detroit also put the finishing touches on a two-year renovation of the offensive line by moving All-Pro Penei Sewell from right tackle to left, adding Cade Mays in free agency and drafting tackle  Blake Miller  with the No. 17 selection.

 

 Otherwise, the team that enters the 2026 campaign is largely made up of the same nucleus that helped push the Lions to so much success. And Detroit has doubled down by locking down two of its young stars in running back Jahmyr Gibbs and linebacker Jack Campbell  with lucrative contract extensions. Those signings followed new deals they've given to other homegrown talents over the past three years and raised their overall investment in extensions to more than $1 billion over that span.

 Dan Campbell said the commitment to the current roster, combined with the organization's recent track record of success, is why he and the Lions remain confident their championship window remains open despite last season's setback.

 "Our window is not closed. It's not closed. That was the whole reason why we did this. We fell short last year. But needed to get in [the playoffs], and now it's about the matchups, where you're playing and who you're playing," Campbell told ESPN of his team, which is  favored by DraftKings to win the NFC North and have the fifth-best odds to win the conference . "We want to be able to do that every year, and sometimes, I'm just saying is what happens is, you want to go all-in for one player, well how do you know that one player doesn't get hurt?

 "Or how do you know the three players behind him don't get hurt and now you've got no depth. Whereas, let's just get a unit together that we feel like can compete every year and then it's about in that moment, we're making those plays and finding a way to win that game."

 And they are not alone in their assessment of the team. Asking about the Lions' prospects revealed a consensus from top coaches around the NFL -- from the  Los Angeles Rams ' Sean McVay to the  Green Bay Packers ' Matt LaFleur -- that the 2026 Lions are not the 9-8 team the league saw last season.

 Here's what the Lions and others around the league are saying about Detroit's Super Bowl worthiness in 2026.

 

 

 Part of the reason for Detroit's uncharacteristic 2025 campaign was the turnover on the coaching staff. After finishing 15-2 in 2024, the Lions most notably lost offensive coordinator Ben Johnson and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn, who took head coaching jobs with the Chicago Bears and the  New York Jets , respectively. Those two departures were big losses for the team. But an underappreciated aspect that contributed to its struggles last season was the sheer number of coaches Campbell had to replace. 

 Campbell: "Well, you learn. But I don't think anybody necessarily tells you, 'Hey, be ready to lose [eight] coaches in one year.' Of course, that's the plan. You're going to lose some guys, you do it right and then the next guy, you can promote or you can go find guys. But when you're talking about [eight coaches], that's a tall task. But you owe it to the players, you owe it to the organization to find the best guy.

 

 "So, I feel like those pieces we added last year, for the most part, really fit what we're about and are good for us."

 McVay: "I think it's a champagne problem. When you end up losing coaches for the reasons that you're talking about with Dan, that means you're doing really well. People want to try to replicate. Or people in your building that are in leadership roles, they want to have them lead or take elevated steps in their career.

 "What I would say is it's a blessing. What I've really leaned into for us is what's been really fortunate is you get exposure to new people. New ideas."

 Glenn: "It's a really good problem to have because usually when you're losing coaches like that, that means you're doing well."

 LaFleur: "I do think that is a challenge, obviously. [Campbell] lost both of his coordinators, and there's a little bit of learning curve there and sometimes you have some growing pains, but I still think they're an elite team."

 

 In Johnson's three years as OC, the Lions established one of the NFL's most dangerous and prolific offenses. In 2024, his unit scored a franchise-record 564 points and led the league in scoring for the first time since 1954. Since 2022 -- the year Johnson took over playcalling duties midseason -- the Lions are tops in the NFL in scoring and total offense. While they still managed 481 points last season, they failed to establish an offensive identity outside of home run plays, and Morton, who replaced Johnson, was relieved of playcalling duties in November. In January, the Lions fired Morton and hired Petzing, who'd spent the previous three seasons as OC of the Cardinals. 

 Campbell: "I feel like the addition with Drew Petzing is going to be great for us. I think it's going to get us centralized. Back to being centralized more on offense."

 McVay: "This league is so volatile, great coaches get let go every year and great coaches become available. And I think when you show your place is a developmental staff that'll invest in the human being and help them get to places that Dan and I were fortunate enough to get to, you attract high-caliber people and you've got to lean into it."

 

 

 The Cardinals ranked second in the NFL in rushing yards per attempt (4.92) and ninth in total rushing yards (6,399) during Petzing's three years of calling plays in Arizona. And while Detroit's average yards per carry remained steady from 2024 to 2025 (4.7 to 4.6), the team's attempts, rushes per game and rushes of 10 or more yards per game all dipped last season. 

 Petzing, on what he wants from his offense in Detroit: "It needs to be physical, it needs to be tough, it needs to be difficult to defend and it needs to be multiple at times.

 "It's not going to all run through one person, it's not going to run through one personnel, it's going to change week to week. I think that's important in this league. Defensive coordinators, I think, do things at a really high level. They watch tape, they understand scheme. So, I think that's a big part of what we need to be on offense."

 Gibbs on Petzing: "He's nice. Smart. He's demanding of us, but he knows we can do it. He puts a lot on our plate, but like I said, he…

title: 2026 Green Bay Packers training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Packers training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Packers reporter Rob Demovsky has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Packers camp. Will the revamped WR corps help QB Jordan Love and the offense take another step? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Packers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news out of Packers camp 
 
 CB Keisean Nixon not guaranteed starting role with Packers 
 Aaron Rodgers wishes game at Lambeau, discusses retirement return 
 Packers QB Love expected to play in first preseason game 
 Micah Parsons: Playing vs. Cowboys in Week 6 'realistic' 
 Packers RT changes last name to Bako-Bewele to honor heritage 
 Packers star TE Tucker Kraft activated off PUP after ACL recovery 
 Packers CEO: Team needs financial bump to stay competitive 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 

 Now we know why edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton had not practiced for more than a week. He experienced a heat-related illness and while the rookie said he wasn't overly concerned about it, the team wasn't taking any chances.

 
"He overheated at practice, so obviously you take that very seriously," coach Matt LaFleur said. "He's kind of working through the protocol to come back."

 
The fourth-round pick had been out since Aug. 10 before he was back on the field Wednesday but was limited to only a few individual drills early in practice.

 
While he wouldn't say whether he had to go to the hospital, Dennis-Sutton said he was treated with IVs and drank fluids. In fact, after his session with reporters in the locker room Wednesday, he drank from a giant jug.

 
Dennis-Sutton was off to a productive start to training camp and had even gotten some rotational work with the No. 1 defense. The Packers are going to need all the pass-rush help they can get early in the season with Micah Parsons expected to start the season on physically unable to perform list while he continues his ACL rehab.

 
"I feel as though I had a really good camp so far, and I just can't wait to get back out there," Dennis-Sutton said. "Right now, I'm just doing what I can, but yeah, feel great, plan to get back."

 

 Other observations: 

 
 Kamal Hadden has taken reps with the No. 1 defense as the slot defensive back in the nickel package this week, and on Wednesday he picked off a Kyle McCord pass. At the end of the play, Hadden got bumped by an offensive player and reacted by spiking the ball after the play. The ball then drilled offensive lineman Dillon Wade . Hadden apologized, saying he had a "PTSD moment" about his gruesome ankle injury from last season. "I just kind of get sensitive running to the left on my ankle and turning back right," Hadden said. "It just gets me in the mode where I'm like, you know, it's kind of unnecessary, but that was all on me, and it shouldn't happen." In fact, he said he and Wade actually sit next to each other in team meetings. "That's my boy," Hadden said, "and I apologize to him for doing that, losing my cool." 
 Despite the interception, McCord has been backing up his strong showing in the preseason opener with some big plays in practice this week. On Wednesday, he had another highlight play when he connected with J. Michael Sturdivant on a deep ball down the right sideline. When asked what the next step for McCord is, LaFleur said: "You've got to repeat that performance each and every week." The Packers might not keep three quarterbacks on the roster, but at the very least, they would like to retain McCord on the practice squad as a developmental prospect. 
 LaFleur said quarterback Jordan Love and the healthy starters will play in Friday's preseason game against the Broncos. Love played one series last week against the Steelers. LaFleur said if all goes according to plan, the starters would not play in the preseason finale against Arizona in part because he expected them to get enough work in next week's joint practice with the Cardinals. 
 All of the players who returned to practice/team drills after extended absences (see Tuesday's practice report) were on the field again Wednesday. That included left guard Aaron Banks (knee), who took some 11-on-11 snaps early in the practice but appeared to have his reps cut short by the end. Running back Josh Jacobs (groin) once again did only individual drills. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 

 One thing that was evident almost immediately in training camp was Zaire Franklin 's intensity. Coach Matt LaFleur noted within the first week that the veteran linebacker "brings it every day."

 That has gone to another level since tight end Tucker Kraft returned to 11-on-11 drills this week.

 
Franklin didn't even remember that he and Kraft got into a scuffle last summer, when the linebacker was with the Colts and they had a joint practice with the Packers, but it's safe to say the tight end brings out the competitiveness in him.

 
Franklin took it up a notch Tuesday. He snagged an interception off a deflection by Edgerrin Cooper in the two-minute drill and then in the next period, he and Kraft barked at each other after Kraft knocked Franklin back as he was trying to get yards after the catch in the right flat.

 
"He's a dog," Franklin said after practice. "That's how it's supposed to be. I feel like with Tuck being out there, I told him, 'I feel like that's what the team is missing.' Like, he brings that same energy, that same competitiveness, that same a--hole mentality that I feel like I bring on the defense. That's what Tuck can do for the offense. So it was great to have him out there, great to compete."

 
It's a different story off the field, though.

 
"We laugh about it," Franklin said. "I think me and Tuck eat breakfast together every morning. I think we could just decide that we're fighting that day, and we still going to eat breakfast together the next morning. So yeah, it's good to have them out there for sure."

 
The Packers traded for Franklin, 30, and then signed him to a restructured contract of two years for $18.01 million after they realized they would not be able to re-sign Quay Walker in free agency.

 
As for Kraft, who is returning from last season's torn ACL, he once again caught every pass thrown his way, including one he pulled in with one hand on the run for a 46-yard touchdown.

 More observations: 

 
 Before practice, LaFleur addressed the recent comments made by Keisean Nixon , who said he thought he was being punished by taking reps with the backups at times. LaFleur said before practice: "The way I look at it is this: then I guess our whole team is being punished because everybody's in competition. I'm a big believer that competition will bring the best out of people. I want everybody to play with the chip on their shoulder. If they feel like they have something to prove, you're probably going to get more out of them." Nixon started at left cornerback with the No. 1 defense, but Benjamin St-Juste and Carrington Valentine also rotated in at that spot. Meanwhile, rookie Brandon Cisse manned the right cornerback spot. 
 Several players did team (11-on-11) drills for either the first time in camp or after an extended absence: left guard Aaron Banks (knee), defensive tackle Javon Hargrave (knee), cornerback Domani Jackson (core) and Valentine (hamstring). Edge rusher Lukas Van Ness returned after missing one open practice because of a shoulder injury.
