full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Jaguars reporter Michael DiRocco has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Jaguars camp. How much will we see Travis Hunter on both sides of the ball in camp? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, concluding with the Jaguars' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Jaguars' camp 
 
 What we've seen from Travis Hunter at Jaguars training camp 
 Sources: Giants agree to trade Daniel Faalele to Jaguars 
 Jaguars' Travis Hunter feeling faster after 10-pound weight gain 
 
 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 
 The Jaguars' red zone offense was rolling against the Carolina Panthers in Wednesday's joint practice at the Miller Electric Center. The first- and second-team offenses at one point scored five touchdowns in a six-play span.

 Trevor Lawrence threw touchdown passes to TE Brenton Strange , TE Nate Boerkircher and WR  Jakobi Meyers  on consecutive snaps. Backup quarterback Nick Mullens also threw a TD pass to TE Tanner Koziol and RB J'Mari Taylor scored on a short outside run around the left side (WR Josh Cameron had a good block on the edge).

 Coach Liam Coen was happy with the physicality the Jaguars showed not only in the red zone period but the entire practice, especially after the slow start the team had in last week's joint practice against the New Orleans Saints .

 "I think that's kind of what we challenged them with a little bit, to come out and set a tone and come out and play fast instead of, all right, we've got to get punched in the mouth and then we respond," Coen said. "So that was nice to see us be able to come out and start fast."

 

 More observations: 

 
 CB/WR Travis Hunter played 28 snaps on defense and two on offense in 11-on-11 work. Had a pass breakup on the sideline on Bryce Young 's pass to TE David Moore . Tight coverage against WR Tetairoa McMillan on another route that ended with a Young throwaway. 
 Hunter also goofed around with K Cam Little and attempted five 27-yard field goals. He missed the first four but hit the last one, which drew a cheer from the crowd and a celebratory dance from Hunter. 
 CB Jabbar Muhammad , who sealed the Jaguars' preseason victory over the Saints with a pass breakup in the end zone, broke up QB Kenny Pickett 's pass to Moore in the end zone during red zone work. 
 DEs Josh Hines-Allen and Danny Striggow had sacks. 
 S Rayuan Lane III forced a Pickett incompletion on a blitz. He hit Pickett's arm, though the contact did not result in any kind of scuffle. 
 Coen said he will decide by Thursday on playing starters against the Panthers in Friday night's game. 
 

 

 Who has been the top performer so far at camp? 
 WR Parker Washington has been QB Trevor Lawrence 's favorite target, and he always seems to be open.

 While the first-team offense has mainly faced the second-team defense in 11-on-11 work, Washington also has thrived in one-on-ones against the Jaguars' top corners. The last time the Jaguars matched the first-team offense against the first-team defense, Washington beat CB Travis Hunter at the line of scrimmage and caught a deep pass down the sideline for a touchdown. Washington, who had three 100-yard games in the final four games (including playoffs) last season, has established himself as the Jaguars' WR1.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 
 Can the offensive line survive a rash of injuries? Starting RT Cole Van Lanen (knee) is still on PUP, starting RG Patrick Mekari (back) has been limited in team work, and key reserve Walker Little (ankle) -- who can start at either tackle and guard spot -- is expected to miss at least another week. The replacements -- notably Chuma Edoga , Jonah Monheim , and Wyatt Milum -- have been up and down, which is to be expected because they're facing the top defensive front.

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Jaguars coach Liam Coen is the offensive playcaller so he naturally wants to see that side of the ball have success in practice. When it doesn't -- which happened on Tuesday -- he's still learning not to get mad.

 The offensive line is dealing with injuries to five players -- including three likely starters -- and as a result struggled to run the ball in 11-on-11 work against what was the top rush defensive in the NFL last season.

 "I thought the defense came out with more energy and better mindset and mentality," Coen said. "Some of the pass game stuff was good, but they kind of took the fight to us for the run game today. We're the No. 1 run defense in the NFL, so it's not going to always be perfect. You're expecting the defense to do some good things, even though it pisses me off at times."

 Tackle Cole Van Lanen (PUP), tackle/guard Walker Little , right guard Patrick Mekari , left guard Ezra Cleveland , and backup left guard Emmanuel Pregnon either did not practice at all or participated only in individual drills. Because the run game struggled so much, Coen decided to cut the practice short. They'll have a light walkthrough on Wednesday and have a joint practice in New Orleans on Thursday.

 "We were supposed to do four-minute [offense] today and go, hit, bang, another four-minute [period] run, run, run, run, run," Coen said. "And the way that those guys came out on defense [and dominated], at the end of the day, I'm the head coach [and] I've got to be happy with something."

 More observations: 

 
 Coen said starters will not play in the preseason opener against New Orleans on Saturday. They will get the majority of the reps in the joint practice against the Saints on Thursday. 
 CB/WR Travis Hunter played 14 snaps in 11-on-11 work (8 defense, 6 offense) and had two catches on three targets. WR Parker Washington beat him off the line of scrimmage and hauled in a deep throw from Trevor Lawrence down the left sideline. 
 

 

 

 Sunday, Aug. 9 
 Head coach Liam Coen is handing over playcalling duty to offensive coordinator Grant Udinski for the preseason games.

 The Jaguars will have a joint practice with the New Orleans Saints on Thursday and two days later will play the Saints at the Caesars Superdome at 4 p.m. ET. Starters are expected to get most of the reps in the joint practice and most will not play against the Saints.

 "Looking forward to it," Udinski said Sunday. "... So we'll put together a call sheet and a game plan accordingly so that way we can see what these guys can do and let them go out there and hopefully compete and have some fun."

 Udinski is in his second season as the Jaguars' offensive coordinator after joining Coen's staff last season following three seasons in Minnesota, moving from the assistant to head coach Kevin O'Connell/special projects in 2022 to the assistant offensive coordinator/assistant quarterbacks coach in 2024.

 Udinski, 30, interviewed for the head coaching jobs in Cleveland and Buffalo in the offseason.

 
 S Eric Murray notched his third interception of camp. Picked off  Trevor Lawrence . 
 Big day for WR Austin Trammell . Had two TD catches from Nick Mullens . Both were deep throws and Trammell made the catches against CB Preston Hodge . 
 S Rayuan Lane III punched the ball away from RB J'Mari Taylor  recovered the fumble. 
 OT Walker Little , TE Quintin Morris , DE Zach Durfee missed Sunday's practice with injuries. DT Arik Armstead had a vet day off. 
 

 

 Friday Aug. 7 
 Parker Washington picked up right where he left off at the end of the 2025 season: As the Jaguars' top pass catcher.

 Washington caught passes for 118 yards and a touchdown in the…

title: 2026 Kansas City Chiefs training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our updates from Chiefs training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Chiefs reporter Nate Taylor has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Chiefs camp. Can coach Andy Reid get the Chiefs back into the playoffs? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, concluding with the Chiefs' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Chiefs stories 
 
 Chiefs' Bieniemy: Wife to make full recovery after being shot 
 Rookie Benson earns shot to start at RT for Chiefs 
 Tight end Travis Kelce says he can still 'play at a high level' 
 Reid: Mahomes unlikely to play in preseason opener 
 Rookie wideout Cyrus Allen an early star of Chiefs training camp 
 
 
 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 

 Mansoor Delane , the Chiefs' rookie cornerback and their top draft pick, is expected to make his preseason debut Saturday night against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers .

 In three consecutive padded practices, Delane has been competitive during man-to-man coverage reps against the Chiefs' top receivers -- such as Rashee Rice , Tyquan Thornton and rookie Cyrus Allen . Before Wednesday's practice, coach Andy Reid expressed how pleased he has been with Delane, who is a projected starter for longtime defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo.

 "You can see the talent," Reid said of Delane. "These next couple of weeks will be good for him. I like what I see. He's definitely not afraid out there -- or hesitant. If anything, you've got to tell him, 'OK, slow down and get those hands off of [the receiver].' He wants to snatch everybody. I mean, we play man [coverage]."

 One change the Chiefs made Wednesday was to have Delane wear mitts on his hands to prevent him from holding receivers during the one-on-one drill. Delane did well in those reps, although Allen was able to make a contested catch on a deep throw from backup quarterback Justin Fields . A few minutes later, Delane had a pass breakup on a shorter route in a rep against Allen.

 "He's a guy who has sticky coverage," defensive backs coach Dave Merritt said of Delane. "Getting him back in pads and seeing that he can actually tackle people now, hopefully that's going to show up this weekend."

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 

 Day after day, the Chiefs' injuries continue to pile up. For the first time in camp, left tackle Josh Simmons missed Tuesday's practice because of a back injury.

 Receivers Tyquan Thornton (strained hamstring) and Jimmy Holiday (quad) left practice early as well. Earlier during Tuesday's on-field work, defensive end Ashton Gillotte , who returned just two days ago following a strained hamstring, sustained a right foot injury while covering tight end Jared Wiley . Linebacker Jack Cochrane missed Tuesday's work with a right knee injury.

 Those players were added to a list that already includes safety Chamarri Conner (sore knee), right guard Trey Smith (hip), cornerbacks L'Jarius Sneed (knee) and Kader Kohou (sore ankle), linebacker Drue Tranquill (lower back spasms) and defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (right knee) who have been held out of practice for much of the past week.

 

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 

 Wearing the usual white jersey for defenders, Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane fully participated in Monday's practice for the first time since camp started.

 Delane missed Saturday's preseason opener as the Chiefs held him out while he continued to let his right shoulder heal, an injury that had led him to wear a noncontact yellow jersey and miss the 11-on-11 reps. In Monday's work, Delane did well to cover receivers such as Rashee Rice , Nikko Remigio and rookie Cyrus Allen . If Delane continues progressing this week, he should make his preseason debut Saturday when the Chiefs face the Tampa Bay Buccaneers .

 "He did everything and was in all the drills," coach Andy Reid said of Delane. "[He] looked good, so that's good work for him as he goes through that. We'll just monitor him and see how he does with the extended play."

 More observations: 

 
 Monday's practice was the Chiefs' longest of camp -- a session that lasted two hours and 15 minutes. Reid said backup left tackle Esa Pole left practice early because he was dehydrated. Receiver Andrew Armstrong sustained a strained hamstring, linebacker Jack Cochrane left early with a knee injury, and undrafted rookie safety DeShon Singleton tweaked a hamstring. 
 Missing practice were right guard Trey Smith (hip), cornerback  L'Jarius Sneed  (rest), linebacker Drue Tranquill (lower back spasms), safety Chamarri Conner (knee) and defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (right knee). "Trey is doing [well]," Reid said. "He's getting close. We'll see where it goes. I don't know if you'll see him this week, but he's getting close. 
 The lone major lineup change among the projected starters was along the offensive line. Kahlil Benson , the undrafted rookie from Indiana, switched from right guard -- the position he played in Saturday's preseason loss to the Los Angeles Rams -- to right tackle. Jaylon Moore , a five-year veteran, switched from right tackle to right guard, the spot where Smith starts. Reid suggested that Benson was moved to get him ready to play the right tackle position in Saturday's exhibition against the Buccaneers. "Moore has been doing a great job in there for us," Reid said. "With that, Benson doesn't get any reps at [right tackle]. We want him to go against the better players and have a chance to continue to grow there. We just flopped them over and let Moore get some reps at guard and Benson gets some reps at the tackle spot. Benson held his own at the guard spot in the game. They need to be able to play both [positions]. It's good experience for them." 
 

 

 

 Who has been the Chiefs' top performer so far at camp? 
 Rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods has been a revelation. Not only has the first-round pick made an impact in each practice, but Woods has quickly shown that he has the quickness and strength to be a potential impact player next to pass rusher Chris Jones . Veterans including center Creed Humphrey , right guard Trey Smith and defensive end George Karlaftis  have praised Woods throughout camp.

 Woods' explosive ability has helped him produce highlight moments in the trenches, whether blowing by Humphrey on a running play or showing off his pass-rush skills in one-on-one drills. Just last week, the 6-foot-3, 310-pound Woods sprinted to chase down Patrick Mahomes , impressing the quarterback.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 

 The lone major position battle is at the right tackle position. Coach Andy Reid is eager to see how Kahlil Benson , the undrafted rookie from Indiana, performs in the preseason.

 The Chiefs have given Benson most of the first-team reps, hoping he can provide true competition to Jaylon Moore , the five-year veteran. If Benson continues to overachieve, even in the preseason -- especially since he's expected to play snaps at right tackle and right guard -- the Chiefs will have to decide if they feel comfortable with him protecting  Patrick Mahomes  despite not having any NFL experience.

 Moore is the safer option, but Benson should have plenty of snaps to demonstrate that he's ready for the spotlight that is opening night on Sept. 14 against the Denver Broncos on "Monday Night Football."

 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 13

title: Inside Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza's game preparation
summary: The rookie QB's studious history shows he'll be ready for Thursday's preseason game at Houston (8 p.m. ET, ESPN).
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Quarterback Fernando Mendoza is a football nerd, but in a good way. Just ask his former high school coach, Dave Dunn.

 As a 15-year-old quarterback at Christopher Columbus High School in Miami, Mendoza would skip eating lunch with his classmates in the cafeteria and take his food to Dunn's office, where he would have a notebook and pen in hand to go over the practice plan.

 Their routine meetings continued throughout Mendoza's time at Christopher Columbus. Even in the offseason, Mendoza would go over what defenses are doing and come up with ideas for the Explorers to implement into their game plan.

 

 "How many 15-year-old kids are wired that way?" Dunn told ESPN.

 Mendoza's meticulous preparation and dedication to his craft propelled him from being a three-star recruit in high school to becoming a Heisman Trophy winner and national champion at Indiana in 2025.

 It is with these traits that the Las Vegas Raiders hope Mendoza can develop into the face of the franchise and help the organization achieve sustained success whenever the 2026 NFL draft's No. 1 pick is called to be the starting quarterback. For now, Mendoza will look to use his studious techniques for Thursday's preseason game against the Houston Texans ( 8 p.m. ET, ESPN ).

 "[At quarterback], the expectation is to be the most prepared guy in the building," Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said. "Out of the young quarterbacks that I have been around, I think he has the upper hand on them in that area."

 Dunn, who has been at Christopher Columbus since 2019 and even coached Mendoza's brother Alberto, said Fernando doesn't like to leave any stone unturned. In Dunn's experience with Mendoza, nothing rarely caught the South Florida native off guard.

 The coach attributed that to Mendoza studying and mentally preparing himself so that he could put the team in the best position to win games. Dunn recalled a moment during a regional final game in which Mendoza didn't see anyone open so he had to improvise and scramble for a touchdown on the first drive.

 

 Mendoza came back to the sideline, breaking down the play, step-by-step.

 "Every once in a while, somebody's going to throw something at you you've never seen before," Dunn said. "... [Mendoza] knew nothing was open, and he knew where the pressure was coming from. He goes, 'All right, I knew I had to move to my left. I had the X receiver as a possibility. Saw that he wasn't going to get open [and] my only option was to scramble.'"

 Dunn admired Mendoza's attention to detail and studious habits. Whenever he saw Mendoza in his office or in team meetings with a notebook, Dunn loved it even if he thought it was out of the norm for younger players.

 Mendoza was even preparing for Kubiak's offensive scheme before he heard his name called in April's draft. Last year in college, he watched a lot of NFL football on Sundays and film breakdowns of how Kubiak utilized the  Seattle Seahawks ' offense.

 Since Mendoza has been a Raider, his notebook is still one of his biggest assets. During Raiders OTAs, quarterbacks coach Mike Sullivan said Mendoza wrote out every pass play, detailing the progression and his footwork. Mendoza even gave his own critique of when he fell short or when he felt he did well.

 

 It was one of the examples Sullivan used to describe Mendoza's tireless work ethic and old-school approach.

 "[Mendoza] didn't have the neatest handwriting, but I appreciated him doing that. I said, 'Maybe you could type this next time,'" Sullivan said. "But he went through that process, and he's someone that I think a lot of his confidence comes from the preparation and the type of time and effort that he puts in."

 Mendoza understands he is behind the curve. Since the start of training camp, Mendoza has mostly played with the second-team offense, while Kirk Cousins has played solely with the starters.

 Last week, Mendoza watched Cousins orchestrate a scoring drive at the beginning of the Raiders' 27-14 preseason loss to the Arizona Cardinals . And he still saw a significant gap between the 15-year veteran signal-caller and himself.

 Still, Mendoza's performance was good enough for Kubiak to call him an "ascending player." He threw for 97 yards and a touchdown, showcasing that progress has been made. Mendoza, however, is a perfectionist, so he harped on his jitters during his first drive, the misthrows and misreads. Mendoza repeatedly mentioned what needs fine-tuning.

 "Like you see Kirk has this time [and] anticipation. ... That's an area I've got to grow in," Mendoza said.

 Mendoza has been putting in extra work outside of the team's training camp practices. He occasionally spends time with the centers on the roster to strengthen his comfort level at playing under center.

 

 He has spent late nights in the indoor practice field, going through the team's offensive script with some of his teammates. And following his preseason debut, Mendoza said he immediately began watching the film of his performance.

 Mendoza continues to be an avid listener, soaking in the advice he receives from Cousins, his coaches and minority owner and NFL legend Tom Brady.

 "You have to do everything that you possibly can to get that mental edge over your opponent, and that's what he's doing," Raiders wide receiver Jalen Nailor said. "He still has a long way to go, but having Kirk as a mentor to him, Tom [Brady] as well, is really going to help his game grow."

 Fullback Connor Heyward said: "He wants to earn everything, which is that much more special. ... When you have a quarterback like that, you know the future is very bright."

 

 Mendoza's short-term memory has also been essential for his development. He tries not to dwell on the mistakes, such as the interception he threw in the red zone to Texans safety Jalen Pitre during the Raiders' joint practice in Houston on Tuesday.

 Instead, he views those moments as learning experiences and maintains an optimistic mindset.

 "It would be letting my teammates down if I let that burden me throughout the next couple of series, because I wouldn't be able to play on time and they wouldn't be able to rely on me," Mendoza said. "Tranquilo, which means 'calm' in Spanish. I say 'tranquilo' and move forward. You know, it's all good."

 Dunn said it has been "surreal" to see Mendoza's rise over time. When Mendoza was an unheralded high school recruit with just one Power 5 offer from Cal, Dunn knew all Mendoza needed was a chance, and his former star player would shine.

 Cal gave Mendoza an opportunity from 2022 to 2024, and then the Hoosiers did in 2025. When the Raiders eventually hand him the keys to the offense, Dunn knows Mendoza will be ready because of the work he puts in.

 "He is a lifelong learner when it comes to football," Dunn said.

title: 2026 Minnesota Vikings training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Vikings training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Vikings reporter Kevin Seifert has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Vikings camp. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Vikings' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Vikings stories 

 
 What Kyler Murray as QB1 means for Vikings, J.J. McCarthy 
 Vikings, O'Neill reach $96M extension 
 Top Vikings storylines after minicamp, from QBs to new GM 
 Will Vikings start Caleb Banks, other rookies on defense? 
 Jefferson says decision on Vikings starting QB 'coach's call' 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 

 J.J. McCarthy took every second-team rep Wednesday in the Vikings' joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens , shortly after coach Kevin O'Connell reiterated with reporters that he considers McCarthy the No. 2 quarterback behind starter Kyler Murray .

 O'Connell, however, said he wants the quarterback position to remain competitive and did not rule out the possibility of  Carson Wentz  challenging McCarthy for the spot.

 
"We want Carson feeling like he can do the things consistently that he can do," O'Connell said, "and that we know exactly who and what he is. And we want J.J. feeling like, 'I'm one snap away, so I've got to prepare like I'm the starter anyway.' It's easy to say those things, but we wanted to have a room that forced it.

 "So we'll see how these next couple of weeks play out, and we're going to do what's best for our team, and proud of the way J.J.'s handled the last few days."

 McCarthy and Murray finished out the team portion of Wednesday's practices with big throws. Murray arced a pass roughly 40 yards into the corner of the end zone, allowing receiver Justin Jefferson to run past a double team and grab the ball for a touchdown. McCarthy then threw about a 30-yard pass over the middle to receiver Myles Price for a score.

 Other observations: 

 
 O'Connell acknowledged there have been some inconsistent snaps from center Blake Brandel to Murray during camp. He indicated it is largely an issue of Brandel anticipating where he is going to step first, triggering an inaccurate snap -- an unsurprising development for a player who hadn't played center before last season. "We have time," O'Connell said, "but not that much time, as I like to say." 
 Quarterback Max Brosmer (right wrist) did some light throwing Tuesday but did not participate in team drills. O'Connell said the Vikings are hoping Brosmer will be ready to play in Saturday's preseason game. 
 Rookie Caleb Tiernan , a third-round draft pick this spring who has been the second-team right tackle during training camp, is week-to-week because of an ankle injury, O'Connell said. 
 

 

 Who is the Vikings' top performer so far at camp? 

 Receiver Tai Felton has demonstrated remarkable improvement from his rookie year, when he struggled to catch the ball consistently in training camp and wound up with a near-exclusive special teams role during the season. He has made one-handed catches in the end zone, demonstrated soft hands at the end of deep routes and displayed his top-end speed while running quick hitters. Coach Kevin O'Connell said he has noted exceptional route running at times as well.

 Is Felton the Vikings' best player? Of course not. But no one has opened more eyes since camp began. He'll push veteran No. 3 receiver Jauan Jennings for playing time.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 

 The entire NFL world wants to know how quarterback Kyler Murray , who was named the starter after a two-week competition with J.J. McCarthy , will perform in the Vikings' offense. But Murray isn't likely to play nearly enough during the preseason to answer that question.

 The most important question the Vikings can realistically answer is how much of their talented draft class will truly be ready to contribute in Week 1.

 That list most notably includes defensive linemen Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange , linebacker Jake Golday , safety Jakobe Thomas , cornerback Charles Demmings and running back Demond Claiborne .

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 

 Second-year quarterback Max Brosmer did not participate in a relatively light practice Monday because of an injured right wrist, a development to keep an eye on as the Vikings prepare for their second preseason game Saturday against the Baltimore Ravens .

 
The Vikings and Ravens are scheduled for two days of joint practices Wednesday and Thursday, and historically coach Kevin O'Connell has not played starters in the preseason game that immediately follows. O'Connell has not revealed his plans for Saturday's game. But assuming that starter Kyler Murray doesn't play, and if Brosmer isn't available, that would leave all the snaps for J.J. McCarthy and Carson Wentz .

 
In 2025, Brosmer played 58% of the Vikings' offensive snaps in the second preseason game following joint practices with the New England Patriots .

 

 Thursday, Aug. 13 

 Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell said earlier this week that both of the quarterbacks who took part in their two-week competition for the starting job would play in Saturday's preseason opener at the New York Giants . That means Kyler Murray will start, along with most of the team's first-team offense, and J.J. McCarthy will play next.

 
The Vikings held a relatively brief practice Thursday, similar to what they would do for a Friday practice during a regular-season week. Two notable veterans did not participate -- receiver Justin Jefferson and left tackle Christian Darrisaw -- making them unlikely to play Saturday.

 
Right guard Will Fries , who had sat out the previous two days of practice, was back on the field and participating in team drills.

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 12 

 While the world has been focused on the Vikings' quarterback competition, another part of their offense has been more quietly under development. 
Coaches are in the process of tweaking the team's run game to give it more variety and, they hope, more production. Once pads came on at the start of the second week of training camp, Vikings running backs have ripped through the line of scrimmage on a regular basis, especially via outside zone concepts. 
"We're running the football very, very well against a really good defense right now," coach Kevin O'Connell said this week. 
On one play Wednesday, running back Jordan Mason followed a block from right tackle Brian O'Neill to reach the sideline and sprint for a touchdown. As Mason was running, O'Neill, right guard Joe Huber and center Blake Brandel sprinted after him in celebration.

 Other observations:

 
 Right guard Will Fries again sat out practice, with Huber taking his place with the first team. 
 Rookie safety Jakobe Thomas participated in individual drills, but his absence from team drills continued. 
 
 

 Tuesday, Aug. 11 

 After his first public practice with the Vikings this spring, Kyler Murray uttered a four-word phrase that hovered over the team's quarterback competition all summer.

 "My confidence," Murray said in May, "is unshakeable."

 That helps explain why Murray didn't sound much different Tuesday after coach Kevin O'Connell named him the team's starter as the third week of training camp began. Murray said he did not expect to be handed the job and acknowledged that not every practice this summer has gone smoothly as he split reps with J.J. McCarthy .

 "There's going to be good days," Murray said. "There's going to be bad days. We're facing adversity every single day. But I'm definitely getting more comfortable as each day…

title: Coach Carter brings old-school toughness to Vikings' O-line
summary: Minnesota's new offensive line coach is pushing players beyond their comfort zone -- and they're buying in.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- It's exhausting just to watch the Minnesota Vikings ' offensive line move through training camp drills.

 The veteran and talented group hits bags, and each other, with a force and intensity that outweighs what's happening at other positions. On an otherwise light day in shells and shorts last week, backup guard Joe Huber hit a bag so hard that it sent backup tackle Henry Byrd to the ground. 

 Some linemen use thick bungee cords to increase the difficulty of their techniques, especially in pass sets. They all run, not walk, back to the group at the end of a rep. When full-team drills begin, all five run to the ball and then run back to the huddle.

 

 At the center of it all is offensive line coach Keith Carter, promoted from assistance O-line coach in February as part of coach Kevin O'Connell's redesign of the run game. Carter is the kind of whirlwind upon which Hollywood script writers could base their archetypal football coach. He's in perpetual motion, "hollering at us," in the words of center Blake Brandel , and "pushing us beyond our comfort zone," according to guard Will Fries .

 Carter keeps the lines moving, with minimal time between reps, and reminds players that "individual drills are not warmups," right tackle Brian O'Neill said.

 "You might not always like it," Fries said, "but it's good for us."

 O'Connell has been clear about what he expects, repeating throughout camp that he wants the line to play "on the other side of the line of scrimmage" after four years of middling physicality. It's hard to imagine a coach more equipped to implement that vision than Carter, whose intensity and physical demands drew public criticism from players at previous stops with the Tennessee Titans (2018-22) and New York Jets (2023-24). 

 

 This summer, ESPN spoke to all five members of the Vikings' starting line about the changes Carter has brought under O'Connell's direction. All five acknowledged camp has been difficult, but they all emphasized that Carter's approach was necessary and appropriate.

 "This is a guy that loves football," O'Neill said. "I mean loves it. Obviously, everyone does if they're in football, but you can just feel it every single day in a walk-through, in a practice, in a meeting. And from a physical standpoint, the bar has been raised a little higher for us. And we knew that was probably going to be the case. 

 "But it's not like we were setting NFL rushing records and protecting the best in the whole entire NFL [in previous seasons]. So if there's a little bit of a different approach, we're going to be receptive to it because we want to be better."

 Carter is the grandson of Pro Football Hall of Fame defensive end Gino Marchetti, and the two shared a close relationship until Marchetti died in 2019. Carter told ESPN that Marchetti helped him develop one of the key tenets of his coaching career. 

 "He told me, 'Keith, make sure that practice is harder than the game.'" Carter said. "'Challenge them at practice, so when they get to the game, they can cut it loose and have fun playing football.'" 

 

 That philosophy, or at least Carter's style in imposing it, did not always sit well with some Titans and Jets players. Former Titans tackle Taylor Lewan wrote in a 2024 Instagram message that he loved the Titans' coaching staff with the exception of Carter. Then-Jets tackle Mekhi Becton and running back Breece Hall appeared to support Lewan's position in subsequent social media comments. 

 The criticisms were not specific, but Lewan ultimately said on the "Bussin' with the Boys" podcast that Carter's approach seemed more like a "dictatorship" when he first arrived in Tennessee. Their relationship ended much better than it started, according to Lewan .

 "Those players saying those things and making those comments," Carter said, "forced me to really dig deep and ask, 'Why do I do what I do? How do I have to communicate with these guys?' So they don't see it as punishment, but they see it as value to the game that they're playing. It's already a hard game, and here I am asking them to make it harder. And so there's so much that goes into it. 

 "I think those comments, they were needed. They've really helped me become a better coach. I hope it shows up in wins and losses this year and how we play. But I know just how it's really helped me to communicate with the guys and keep me grounded to why I do what I do, and not let some of the other stuff get in the way of that."

 Left tackle Christian Darrisaw nodded his head vigorously this week when asked if Carter's explanations have landed. 

 "Absolutely," he said. "I see no ill intentions coming from anything like that. He pushes us hard, but we know the intentions behind it, the details and just the things that he's coaching us on. You kind of sometimes need that refresher.

 "All the things that you hear around the league, and then being on the practice field with him since April, he's not that guy. We know he might get on us, but we know the purpose and the intention that's coming from him."

 

 If anything, Vikings linemen wanted to be coached harder.

 "I love that approach to the game," Brandel said. "What's most important is violence and speed and effort, and that's what he really coaches us on."

 Said left guard Donovan Jackson : "He brings the juice every day. His philosophy is a little bit different than maybe some other coaches, but it's O-line play. It's going to be physical regardless."

 The impact of Carter's approach has stood out numerous times since the start of camp. During a full-pads practice last week, O'Neill, Huber and Brandel could be seen sprinting behind running back Jordan Mason after he broke free on an outside zone run. The point, Carter said, is clear.

 "If you were to break down the job of an offensive lineman," Carter said, "it's to protect the guy with the ball. So as long as there's somebody with a ball in their hands still running, we believe our job is to continue to block or go protect him when he's getting tackled."

 On the first play of Saturday's preseason game, running back Aaron Jones Sr. gained 18 yards in part because Darrisaw drove New York Giants defensive lineman Darius Alexander 5 yards downfield. Five plays later, Mason gained 15 yards in part because Fries pushed the Giants' Leki Fotu from one hashmark to the other, creating a gaping hole for Mason to run through. 

 "That little bit that we were able to showcase," Fries said, "it makes it kind of exciting to see what we can do over the course of the whole season."

 O'Connell hired Carter as an assistant offensive line coach prior to the start of the 2025 season, saying he was a "tough, kind of gritty guy" and acknowledged reporters would "find something about him in regards to being tough on his players."

 But he said he thought Carter would be "really good for us." In promoting him to replace the fired Chris Kuper in February, O'Connell said that he spent the 2025 season getting to know Carter, as well as giving him a chance to learn the players and "really have a full-scale understanding of how to individually coach" each one.

 "I've had nothing but a good experience so far playing for him," Fries said. "I'm a believer in what I think, and what I see, and I want to give everyone the benefit of the doubt. Nobody's perfect. If you ask anybody, have they made mistakes in their past? Absolutely. I know I have.

 "And I think that if you're able to learn from those things that you want to get better at, it makes you better as a person, as a man, as a coach. And I think that we've seen that in him."

full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Patriots reporter Mike Reiss has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Patriots camp. Will Drake Maye  start another MVP-like campaign in Year 3? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Patriots' Brown knows Vrabel's rip comes from 'great place'

 Too many receivers? A look at the Patriots' crowded WR room 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 
 On the first snap the Patriots and Eagles were on the field together, wide receiver A.J. Brown ran a go route against cornerback Quinyon Mitchell and had a chance to electrify the estimated crowd of 12,000-plus.

 Brown created separation, fought through a potential penalty, but then failed to secure the catch.

 It was the only blemish on a productive day in which Brown totaled six receptions against his former team.

 "Q got away with a little holding," Brown said with a laugh, when asked to describe the play against Mitchell. "I won, he pulled himself back into the play, and I just have to finish the play. My right hand didn't get to the ball quick enough. My left hand got on the ball. That's on me. Attention to detail -- catching the ball high, not letting it get low.

 "... It's never about who I'm going against, it's the little things; that could have been a 40-yard bomb, but now it's a long foul ball. Those are the things I'm focusing on."

 Brown met with reporters after practice and upon his arrival he took note of seeing "old friends" in the media from spending four seasons in Philadelphia. He said he hasn't spoken with Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts since the trade, but he had "all love" for his time in Philadelphia.

 As for how he feels things are going learning to work with a new quarterback in Drake Maye , he said: "There have definitely been some challenges but he's very special. He makes my job a lot easier. There's a learning curve and we'll continue to keep working at it."

 

 More observations: 

 
 One area of improvement from last week's practice with the Colts came in the two-minute drill. The Patriots' top offense rushed Andy Borregales on for a successful field goal, while the top defense held the Eagles without points.  Although not facing a pass rush that can tackle him, Maye was accurate and in rhythm for the most part. One charting of his day had him 16-of-19 in 11-on-11 work. 
 Rookie OLB Gabe Jacas was elevated to the first unit on punt protection, and said after practice he has never executed those responsibilities prior to coming to New England. Coach Mike Vrabel has been spending one-on-one time with him. 
 Newly signed veteran G/C Greg Van Roten initially worked at center with the second unit in warmups. 
 Starting CB Christian Gonzalez has remained out of practice since Aug. 11. 
 There were no fights, as the professionalism of both teams showed up. The lone dust-up came after a snap in a FG drill and Vrabel got right in the middle of it to help extinguish things quickly. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 Former Patriots wide receiver Julian Edelman was a guest of the team's light, low-tempo practice. Edelman watched from the sideline and at one point was chatting with owner Robert Kraft.

 "It's always good to have Patriots legends around here," veteran tight end Hunter Henry said. "The more the merrier. Those guys set the standard here, so it's always good to have them back."

 Edelman also caught up with wide receiver A.J. Brown , who will be under the spotlight the next two days with the Eagles coming to town for two practices. Edelman had given Brown his blessing to wear his old No. 11, but Brown previously said he wanted to honor Edelman's legacy and create his own by wearing No. 1 (his old college number).

 The Patriots officially signed veteran G/C Greg Van Roten to a one-year deal and released TE Mitch Van Vooren . The 36-year-old Van Roten, who projects as the top interior backup with Ben Brown sidelined multiple weeks due to injury, has been assigned jersey No. 70. 
 Veteran LB Robert Spillane was one of the last players on the field after practice, as he spent time working with 2026 second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas on punt protection and punt-rush technique. 
 As for what to expect in Wednesday and Thursday practices with the Eagles, coach Mike Vrabel said: "I think upwards of probably 28 reps, 30 reps for the first group on each day is a good number ... we'll be able to do a lot more field work on the first day and then probably focus on the red zone the next day." 
 The Patriots had veteran free agent DT DaQuan Jones and veteran free agent LB Shaq Thompson in for visits (different from tryouts). 
 
 

 Monday, Aug. 17 
 Quarterback Drake Maye  delivered a beautiful deep pass to receiver A.J. Brown for a 65-yard(ish) touchdown over the middle, which was the highlight play of practice.

 Maye thrust his right arm into the air in celebration, with his right index finger extended. A few yards behind him, coach Mike Vrabel did the same.

 The play, and celebration, served as a fitting preview for what is to come: Brown's former team, the Eagles, visiting New England for practice on Wednesday and Thursday. Brown is scheduled to address reporters after Wednesday's practice.

 Maye and Brown have been working behind the scenes, and on the field, to develop a connection. Their lockers are next to each other. Brown also said they often sit next to each other in meetings.

 Some of their best work leading into Monday has been in the red zone, where Brown's size (6-foot-1, 226 pounds) and physicality have shown up. They hadn't experienced consistent success on the deep ball before Monday, which might have explained the emphatic reactions from Maye and Vrabel.

 More observations: 

 
 In a rare drill that fourth-year DT Cory Durden said he's never seen before in the NFL, the team gathered on one field and rookies and first-year players were challenged to one-on-one drills as everyone watched. One highlight was first-round pick Caleb Lomu (right tackle) blocking second-round pick Gabe Jacas (outside linebacker). "Coach was giving them an opportunity to perform in front of their teammates. It's a pride thing," Durden said. "It brings energy to everybody. Nobody wants to lose in front of the whole team." 
 Kicker Andy Borregales was once again challenged in a full-team field goal drill by kicking into skinny posts (about half the width of regulation goal posts). Two days after going 6-of-6, he was 3-of-5 from a distance between 37 and 52 yards. The two misses were estimated to have been successful on regular goalposts. 
 Starting LB Christian Elliss and reserve OLB Jesse Luketa left the full-pads practice early, while starting DT Christian Barmore returned.

title: How will the Patriots respond in 2026 to the Super Bowl loss?
summary: After an eventful offseason with much roster turnover, New England is again focusing on identity to combat a harder schedule this season.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- The New England Patriots didn't even need to play a preseason game before meeting their new reality.

 The Indianapolis Colts arrived at the Patriots' practice fields last week -- where the energy of 10,000-plus cheering and booing fans put a palpable football buzz in the air -- and turned up the intensity.

 When Indianapolis intercepted quarterback Drake Maye on his final pass, then carved up the Patriots' top defense with ease to score a touchdown, the Colts celebrated as if they had won something big .

 "It's being able to go against the former AFC champions and measure where we are," Colts safety Cam Bynum explained.

 Ready or not, New England, this is what life is like at the top of the AFC.

 The Patriots are no longer the upstart; instead, just like the majority of the Bill Belichick/Tom Brady years, they are the team others in the conference are targeting after their surprise run to Super Bowl LX , which they lost decisively to the Seattle Seahawks  29-13.

 A lot has happened since then, including an offseason dominated by coach Mike Vrabel's personal travails , a long-rumored trade for star wide receiver A.J. Brown and nearly unprecedented roster turnover for a conference champion. It set the stage for the question many are asking: Are the Patriots primed to succumb to a tougher schedule or will Vrabel's relentless commitment to establishing team identity deliver another surprising run to the Super Bowl?

 

 "Having a taste of that game, being there, feeling that, feeling all the feels when you don't get what you want, it makes you hungry," New England linebacker and team captain Robert Spillane said of the Super Bowl defeat. "It makes you second-guess everything you've done. It makes you look for a little bit more of an edge."

 Indianapolis gave the Patriots an early taste of how opponents will be raising their intensity level against them, even if DraftKings Sportsbook doesn't view New England as the AFC favorite at +1600 (tied for third, behind the  Buffalo Bills  and the  Baltimore Ravens ). But the Patriots have a chance to prove what kind of team they will be when they open the season in Seattle on Sept. 9 (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC).

 "Knowing where you are, and what type of team you are, is very important," said fifth-year cornerback and punt returner  Marcus Jones . "We are the team being hunted. We have to wear that chip on our shoulder every time we get out there."

 
 MAYE SAT AT the interview podium for 16 minutes following February's Super Bowl loss in Santa Clara, California. His eyes welled up. His voice cracked at times.

 The first thing he said: "It hurts."

 The heartbreak set the stage for his offseason, which was already being mapped out that night.

 "That's what fuels you," Maye said. "I think that's the biggest thing about life. You're going to have times like this. It's how you bounce back."

 Vrabel kept repeating "307" to players in the aftermath, a reference to the number of days they had been together as a team and how far they had come in a short time. He told them to be prepared for a quick turnaround for the start of the voluntary offseason program in late April.

 By April, the Patriots were a much different team, a result of being aggressive spenders in free agency for a second straight year.

 Former  Green Bay Packers  wide receiver Romeo Doubs was a big catch and signed a four-year, $68 million free agent deal after the team released 2025 leading receiver Stefon Diggs . At outside linebacker, veteran Dre'Mont Jones (three years, $36.5 million) was prioritized over retaining pass rusher K'Lavon Chaisson (career-high 7.5 sacks in 2025), in part because Jones is a sturdier option against the run.

 

 Veteran safety Kevin Byard , who led the NFL with seven interceptions in 2025 with the  Chicago Bears , was considered a coup and the reason the Patriots elected not to re-sign starter Jaylinn Hawkins (now with the Ravens). Guard Alijah Vera-Tucker  also was brought aboard (three years, $42 million), which led to a trade of starting center Garrett Bradbury (1,072 snaps played) to the Bears and 2025 third-round pick Jared Wilson sliding over to replace him. Fullback Reggie Gilliam (three years, $10.8 million) was another early signing, which highlighted the desire to become a tougher, more physical team in the run game and on kickoff returns -- roles in which Gilliam excelled with the Bills.

 After what seemed like a successful free agency, the Patriots were preparing for the NFL draft when the discourse surrounding the team and its head coach took a turn.

 On April 7, the New York Post published pictures of Vrabel and The Athletic NFL reporter Dianna Russini at a luxury resort in Arizona, appearing to show the two, who are both married, embracing and holding hands days before the NFL spring league meetings. Russini resigned from The Athletic on April 14. One week later, Vrabel addressed reporters for the first time, calling it a "personal and private matter" and saying, "I've had some difficult conversations with people I care about -- with my family, the organization, the coaches, the players."

 As part of the fallout, Vrabel was away from the team on April 25, the third and final day of the NFL draft, as he said he was beginning the process of seeking counseling . The Patriots made six of their nine overall selections that day with the coach absent.

 They aren't relying on major contributions from their draft class, as Utah offensive tackle Caleb Lomu (first round, No. 28), Illinois outside linebacker Gabe Jacas (second round, No. 55) and Notre Dame tight end Eli Raridon (third round, No. 95) currently project as top backups and Wake Forest cornerback Karon Prunty (fifth round, No. 171) as a core special teams player.

 Vrabel's situation lingered throughout May before the Patriots made headlines once again -- this time trading for Brown, the Philadelphia Eagles ' star wide receiver.

 Speculation of a trade had been stirring for months, but it was officially announced June 1. The Patriots sent their 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick to deliver Maye a clear-cut No. 1 target and address perhaps the top deficiency on the roster.

 Brown, who grew up a Patriots fan, instantly shifted the energy around the team with his arrival. Smiling at the interview dais, he famously said, "Obviously, I know this ain't heaven, but it's close to it."

 

 Offensive tackle Morgan Moses , New England's oldest (35) and longest-tenured player (13th season), sounded optimistic that the Patriots can turn the page on last season and build with new additions.

 "You live and you learn. What we did last was successful, but obviously, we didn't walk off with the [Lombardi] Trophy like we wanted to," he said. "You gotta learn how to lose before you can win. I think we've digested that well over the offseason and coming together, adding new pieces."

 
 WITH PLENTY OF new faces in the locker room, Vrabel sought to continue what worked well in 2025: building a team identity.

 On Aug. 4 in the Patriots' new 160-seat auditorium, he stood in front of his players and talked about oranges and how the fruit relates to what he wants the 2026 Patriots to ideally become.

 Yes, oranges. 

 Vrabel explained: When an orange is squeezed, everyone knows what it creates. So, when the Patriots are in the juicer, such as in a competitive game in a pressure-filled fourth quarter, can they become a team that oozes the ingredients most important to Vrabel?

 "Whatever you squeeze is what you are. That's you. He's trying to pull that out of us," veteran punter Bryce Baringer said.

 "He made the analogy if someone squeezes an orange, watermelon juice isn't going to come out. So, when we're squeezed, we have to be that team; it needs to be those four pillars of our identity."

 The four pillars haven't changed since last season: effort and finish; ball security and disruption; details, techniques and fundamentals;…

title: Can Adonai Mitchell be 'Robin' that Jets are searching for?
summary: New York has struggled to find a complement to Garrett Wilson since drafting him in 2022.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- In  Garrett Wilson 's first four seasons with the New York Jets , his opening-day sidekicks at wide receiver were, chronologically:

 Corey Davis , Allan Lazard, Mike Williams and Josh Reynolds .

 One got benched (Lazard), one got traded (Williams) and one got injured (Reynolds). None of them caught more than 32 passes.

 Next tag-team partner up: Adonai Mitchell .

 

 "If he continues on this trajectory right here," receivers coach Shawn Jefferson said of Mitchell, "he will be a really good Robin for our Batman. Big time."

 Except for an 11-game stretch in 2024, when Davante Adams was acquired in a trade that reunited him and Aaron Rodgers , Gotham City has lacked a dynamic duo at receiver in recent years. The franchise that produced star tandems such as Wayne Chrebet-Keyshawn Johnson (1990s) and Al Toon-Wesley Walker (1980s) has fielded its share of jokers.

 In Mitchell, the Jets believe they have an ascending talent, ready to pop in his third year in the NFL -- a player whose outside vertical speed should complement Wilson's slipperiness in the short and intermediate areas.

 Since 2022, the Jets have relied on Wilson and running back Breece Hall as their offensive staples, hoping each year to uncover a third option -- either a No. 2 wide receiver or a pass-catching tight end.

 Hall said he and Wilson have a friendly competition, trying to outdo each other for the unofficial title of "best player on offense." They'd love it if their two-man show turned into a three-man battle. Did someone say four?

 "I believe we have the pieces in place that will get us to playing meaningful football in December, something I've dreamed about doing for a long time," said Wilson, who, like Hall, has yet to experience a winning season in the green and white.

 Hall believes this is the best and most cohesive skill-position group they've had during their tenure, saying, "We feel we finally have a team around us for us to really flourish and do what we know we can do."

 To be fair, the Wilson-Adams-Hall troika produced solid numbers, if not victories, in 2024 -- a 5-12 season. In fact, Wilson set career highs in catches (101), receiving yards (1,104) and touchdowns (seven), in part, because Adams was able to draw coverage away from him. That they got competent quarterback play from Rodgers also was a factor.

 

 Adams was productive (67 catches for 854 yards in 11 games), but he was perceived as a hired gun, just passing through to satisfy Rodgers' desire for another weapon. The Mike Williams experiment backfired, leading to the Adams trade.

 This time, the candidates for the "Robin" role have a chance to stick around for a while. Mitchell, acquired from the Indianapolis Colts in last season's Sauce Gardner blockbuster trade, is signed through 2027. Tight end Mason Taylor is under contract through 2028. Tight end Kenyon Sadiq and wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr ., both 2026 first-round picks, are signed through 2029.

 Hall and Wilson are locked up through 2028 and 2030, respectively, so you can see why Hall has talked about having stability and continuity for a change. In theory, the group will grow together, presumably with a long-term quarterback solution arriving in 2027.

 The key is player development. Hall and Wilson are the only proven players; the others still are feeling their way through the early stages of their careers. Growing pains are likely.

 Which brings us back to Mitchell, the most experienced of the bunch -- a 2024 second-round pick with 56 receptions in three seasons. In Indianapolis, he was inconsistent, had some drops and lost playing time before being shipped to New York.

 Initially perceived as a "throw in" in the Gardner trade, in which the Jets also received two first-round picks, Mitchell actually was a prime target for the front office. No Mitchell, no deal. He flashed a little last season (24 catches in eight games for the Jets) and became the talk of the offseason, settling into the team and raising expectations.

 "A new start, a new beginning, new quarterback, new system," Mitchell said. "I mean, I love it. I love the challenge. I love embracing what we have here."

 In the offseason, Mitchell hopped on a flight and flew to Miami to work out with newly-acquired quarterback Geno Smith . For five days, Mitchell, Smith and Taylor powered through oppressive heat and humidity in an effort to build chemistry before training camp.

 Early in camp, Hall named Mitchell, Taylor, Sadiq and running back Braelon Allen as the four players that could help lift the offense to a higher level -- which is to say, out of the basement. They finished 29th in scoring, their 10th straight year in the bottom 10.

 

 Sadiq hasn't been available; he has missed the last eight practices because of a setback from offseason hernia surgery. He's expected to return by Week 1, but it's fair to wonder about residual effects from the layoff.

 Taylor and Allen are having good camps, with Allen's role increasing now that Hall (strained groin) is out for two to three weeks , according to coach Aaron Glenn. And let's not forget about Cooper. The Jets thought enough of him to trade into the bottom of the first round, but he's been up and down.

 Playing with the backups, Cooper made two catches for 31 yards against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the preseason opener Friday, but his role for the regular season is uncertain. He has lost reps to Isaiah Williams , the biggest surprise in camp. Williams is drawing effusive praise from the coaches. Cooper is experiencing "little pitfalls," according to Jefferson -- not uncommon for a rookie.

 Still, there is optimism.

 "It feels different this year," Wilson said. "It just does."

 Call it a Bat signal.

 Catch up on all the updates, concluding with the Jets' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Jets camp 
 
 RB Breece Hall strains groin, Glenn says its not serious 
 Jets CB Stiggers taken to hospital after collapsing at practice 
 No. 2 pick Bailey living up to hype, bringing 'juice' to Jets 
 Rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq to miss time after hernia setback 
 Jets' Smith rues being 'distraction' after dispute with girlfriend 
 2026 Jets training camp preview 
 
 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 

 Upset that Cade Klubnik played only two series last week in the preseason opener? Want to see the rookie quarterback in a longer stint?

 Well, you probably will get your wish this week, and don't be surprised if he starts again. The Jets face the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday night at Acrisure Stadium.

 With Geno Smith still dealing with an ankle injury -- it was heavily taped for practice -- coach Aaron Glenn remained noncommittal on his QB choice. Out of caution, he could sit Smith for the second straight game even though he hasn't missed a full practice.

 "I've never been a coach that was afraid of injuries because it's part of the game, but I also want to be a coach that's smart and make sure I get our guys ready for Week 1," Glenn said.

 Klubnik, who led the offense to 10 points in his two-series debut, appears to be in line for a bigger role this week.

 Rebounding from an uneven practice Tuesday, the former Clemson star was sharp, especially during the red zone period. He went 3-for-3, with passes to Garrett Wilson , Jelani Woods (TD) and Kene Nwangwu (TD). In previous practices, he had experienced some hiccups in the red area.

 "I think every time he practices, he's getting better and better and better," said Glenn, adding that Klubnik has the aptitude to learn from his mistakes.

 Barring something unforeseen, Klubnik appears to have locked up the No. 2 job.

 Other observations: 

 
 The defense controlled the early part of an abbreviated practice. DE  Will McDonald IV  (sack), DT Jowon Briggs (tackle for loss) and S Dane Belton (pass breakup) made splash plays while the entire unit stymied Smith (0-for-3) and the passing attack. 
 The kicking competition between Jason Sanders and Cade York is difficult to call, but it's clear that York has the stronger leg. 
 The defense is putting an emphasis on takeaways. Makes sense, considering the ignominy of 2025 -- first team in history to go an entire season without intercepting a pass. The goal is three picks a day in practice, according to nickelback Jarvis Brownlee Jr ., who said the defense faces "consequences" if it comes up short. The consequences are post-practice gassers. 
 Good news: CB Qwan'tez Stiggers , who was diagnosed with a concussion last week after passing out on the sideline, returned to practice on a limited basis (red concussion jersey). 
 An extreme example of load management -- backup MLB Kiko Mauigoa received a veterans' rest day. Mind you, he's a second-year player, only 23 years old. Explaining the decision, Glenn noted that Mauigoa had logged more practice reps in camp than perhaps any player on defense. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 

 Quarterback Geno Smith , learning a new system, said it's "very important" for him to play in the preseason. But he wouldn't take it further, saying the decision belongs to coach Aaron Glenn.

 Smith is dealing with a sore left ankle. He hasn't missed any practice time, but he was scratched from the preseason opener last Friday. On Tuesday, Glenn was noncommittal on whether Smith would play Friday night against the Pittsburgh Steelers .

 Every other offensive starter played last week. Ideally, Smith would get a couple of series against the Steelers for the sake of timing and chemistry.

 Smith is accustomed to playing in the preseason. He played 28 snaps last summer for the Las Vegas Raiders . In his final two preseasons with the Seattle Seahawks , 2023 and 2024, he played a combined total of only 17 snaps.

 "I'll leave it up to coach, but my job is to get ready and help this team get ready to be ready to play Week 1," Smith said. "Whenever I get the chance to play, I look forward to it. I'll also leave that up to coach."

 Smith, commenting for the first time on his ankle injury, was tightlipped. He wouldn't say how it happened, except to say, "I just had some swelling, swelling in my ankle." It developed during last week's joint practices with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers .

 For what it's worth, the sleeve on his lower left leg was gone for practice.

 Other observations:  

 
 Rookie QB Cade Klubnik threw a couple of interceptions in practice, one on a pass that was tipped by Will McDonald IV and picked off by Azareye'h Thomas and another on a ball that was dropped by Chip Trayanum and intercepted by  Samuel Womack III . 
 With the injuries to Breece Hall (groin) and Isaiah Davis (knee), Trayanum and Sam Scott -- both rookie free agents -- are getting extra reps. Scott, out of Wyoming, has had some impressive moments. 
 A handful of Jets' legends watched practice, including Vinny Testaverde, Kevin Mawae and Keyshawn Johnson -- members of the 1998 team that reached the AFC Championship Game. 
 Rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq (hernia) and rookie CB D'Angelo Ponds (calf) are inching closer to returning. They're expected to be ready for Week 1, according to Glenn. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 

 It was a rough way to end practice.

 RB Breece Hall was in the locker room, nursing a groin injury from earlier in practice. WR Garrett Wilson was nowhere to be found; he showed up sick in the morning, vomiting, and was held out. QB Geno Smith was on the field, taking his full share of reps, but he was favoring his left ankle -- an injury that occurred Wednesday and kept him out of the preseason opener Friday.

 Not a great day for the Jets' big three on offense.

 Smith powered through the relatively light practice, though he did have one hiccup -- an overthrow that was picked off by S Andre Cisco in a two-minute drill.

 Coach Aaron Glenn acknowledged that Smith still is feeling the residual effects of the injury, adding, "I want to see exactly how he feels coming out of this practice to see how we're going to continue to move forward."

 Something to watch. Rookie Cade Klubnik started the opener and played well.

 Other observations:  

 
 There was some positive injury news, as NT T'Vondre Sweat and edge  Joseph Ossai practiced for the first time. Both are projected starters. "We want to make sure we take our time with [Sweat]," Glenn said of the 360-pounder. 
 The cornerback room has absorbed some hits. Nahshon Wright (undisclosed), Qwan'tez Stiggers (concussion) and rookie D'Angelo Ponds (calf) didn't practice. Ponds, who was expected to compete for a starting job, still hasn't practiced. Rookie free agent Mory Bamba , who recorded four passes defensed in the opener, injured a knee in the game and will be sidelined at least two weeks. 
 WRs Isaiah Williams and rookie Omar Cooper Jr . stayed after practice for about an hour, each catching about 100 balls from the JUGS machine. They also caught tennis balls and bean bags. Williams, known for his kickoff and punt return abilities, said he wants to improve his hands. 
 Despite two consecutive days with no practice, LB  Demario Davis  and S Minkah Fitzpatrick received veteran rest days. Load management is one of the themes in camp.…

title: 2026 Philadelphia Eagles training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our updates from Eagles training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Eagles reporter Tim McManus has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and -- of course -- the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Eagles camp. How will quarterback  Jalen Hurts fare in the reimagined offense? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Eagles news 
 
 Moro Ojomo, Fred Johnson scuffle at Eagles camp 
 Eagles QB Jalen Hurts' speed in camp drawing rave reviews 
 Epenesa grateful to be Eagle after 'weird' Browns situation 
 Eagles' Nolan Smith apologizes for 'unacceptable' speeding arrest 
 Eagles, DT Carter agree to four-year, $152M extension 
 

 
 Wednesday, Aug. 19 
 Day 1 of the Eagles-Patriots joint practices did not disappoint. Wide receiver  A.J. Brown was the focal point, and the session started with a battle with corner Quinyon Mitchell during one-on-ones, which ended in an incompletion deep down the left sideline. Brown said with a smile afterwards that Mitchell got away with a hold.

 Brown cleaned up from there, though, hauling in all six passes that went his way during 7-on-7 and team drills. The highlight was a beauty of a deep ball down the right sideline by quarterback  Drake Maye . Brown was able to beat cornerback  Riq Woolen at the line of scrimmage and hauled in the pass at the boundary. Overall, the Eagles' first-team defense had a difficult time slowing Maye and the Patriots' first-team offensive attack.

 Other observations:  

 
 
 It was a mixed bag for QB Jalen Hurts . He threw multiple interceptions but also had arguably his best pass of the summer -- a dime deep down the left side for WR  Elijah Moore , who hauled in the catch and then tossed the ball in the air in celebration.

 
 
 The interior offensive line was giving up too much pressure against a stout Patriots front. That would be problematic if it continues into regular season game action.

 
 
 Receivers DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon (hamstring) were both listed as limited. Lemon mostly worked off to the side but is moving better than we have seen since sustaining the injury early on in camp.

 
 

 

 
 Monday, Aug. 17 
 Eagles No. 1 receiver DeVonta Smith returned to the practice field after sitting out the previous seven sessions because of a hamstring injury. Smith was a limited participant but looked like his normal self -- explosive, quick getting in and out of breaks -- during individual drills. Monday also marked the return of corners Quinyon Mitchell (glute) and  Cooper DeJean  (groin).

 Rookie receiver Makai Lemon (hamstring) sat out his eighth straight practice but has been ramping up his side work over the past handful of days.

 More observations: 

 
 Quarterback Jalen Hurts and the offense had an unremarkable day. Hurts didn't throw downfield much. One pass he did let fly was intercepted by Michael Carter II , who got good positioning on Quez Watkins to make the play. 
 Hurts was able to connect with Hollywood Brown for a chunk gain. Brown found a pocket in the defense between Zack Baun and Riq Woolen and Hurts zipped it in. 
 

 

 

 Who is the Eagles' top performer so far at camp? 

 WR Darius Cooper . No one has made more of their opportunities than Cooper, the 2025 undrafted free agent out of Tarleton State. He came out of nowhere to make the team as a rookie and is making another strong push this summer, standing out in a deep group that includes Hollywood Brown , Elijah Moore and Dontayvion Wicks . Hamstring injuries have sidelined both DeVonta Smith and rookie Makai Lemon for most of camp. Cooper has stepped in and has developed good rapport with QB  Jalen Hurts while showing off strong hands and a willingness to go over the middle.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 
 How will the offensive operation look? The starters are expected to sit out the preseason but there is still plenty to learn about how things function under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion . He has never called plays and has yet to commit to whether he'll be doing so from the booth or the sideline on game days. The team's hope is the offense is quick out of the huddle, light on penalties and looks efficient during Mannion's test-drive.

 

 Thursday, Aug. 13 
 Quarterback Jalen Hurts had an up-and-down day. He was intercepted by CB Mac McWilliams on an end-zone fade to Hollywood Brown during 7-on-7s early in practice. He got into a flow as the session went on, though, hitting Elijah Moore and Dontayvion Wicks in rhythm before connecting with tight end Dallas Goedert over the middle for a touchdown. Later, Hurts and Wicks hooked up for a touchdown in the corner of the end zone over Riq Woolen , who has come back to earth some this summer following a highly-productive spring.

 More observations:  

 
 Someone should block linebacker  Jalyx Hunt . He's come free far too many times this camp, including from the left side on Thursday to blow up the play. 
 Cooper DeJean (groin) and Quinyon Mitchell (glute) were both sidelined. They were replaced in the lineup by McWilliams and Michael Carter II , respectively. 
 Brown dropped a short pass from Hurts in the red zone. The competition feels tight further down the receiver depth chart, with Darius Cooper , Moore, Brown, Britain Covey and Johnny Wilson among those hoping to find their way onto the 53-man roster. 
 

 
 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 Quarterback Jalen Hurts and receiver Elijah Moore connected for another big play on Tuesday.

 Hurts uncorked a deep shot for Moore, who sped past safety  Andre' Sam  and hauled in the pass for a touchdown. Moore celebrated by punting the ball well over the practice field gate.

 Hurts has been without DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon the past six practices because of hamstring injuries but is finding a lot of value in building chemistry with some of the other receivers.

 Moore is one of the primary players capitalizing on that opportunity, generating a number of highlight plays alongside QB1.

 More observations: 

 
 Cornerback Quinyon Mitchell sat out of team drills after pulling up during a one-on-one rep against Hollywood Brown . Mitchell went to the sideline and had his right leg stretched out by a trainer. Mac McWilliams took over for him with the first team. 
 Reserve corner Jakorian Bennett has had a good number of pass breakups this summer. He had another one on a Hurts attempt for Moore down the right seam on Tuesday. 
 Cooper DeJean came up with an interception on a reckless downfield throw from Andy Dalton . Later, DeJean blitzed Hurts and registered the "sack." 
 Edge rusher Jalyx Hunt has been one of the more impressive players on the field during camp. He came clean on one rush and chased Hurts to the other side of the field, eventually forcing him out of bounds. 
 
 

 Monday, Aug. 10 
 Eagles cornerback Quinyon Mitchell came up with his second interception of camp -- perhaps foreshadowing a breakout year for him in the takeaway department. Mitchell sniffed out a Jalen Hurts pass intended for Hollywood Brown over the middle and came up with the pick on the first play of a simulated two-minute drive.

 
"Just his patience, his confidence," CB Riq Woolen said on what stands out about Mitchell. "He's been in this defense ... so he has a good understanding of how he can play certain techniques and certain coverages. Being able to watch him make plays, it inspires me to make plays."

 
Mitchell, a first-team All Pro in 2025, has yet to record a regular-season interception in his two years in the league but is tied for the most career playoff interceptions (four) among active…
